title: What government is and does
description: Government is the system by which a country or community is run: it makes laws, keeps order, defends, provides services and raises taxes. The word comes from the Greek for steering a ship.

facts.text: The word 'govern' comes, through Latin gubernare, from the Greek kybernan, meaning to steer or pilot a ship.
Government is the political system by which a country or community is administered and regulated: how a society organizes itself and allocates authority.
Governments make laws to keep order, provide defense, police and fire services, provide benefits such as education, health care and roads, and raise money through taxes.

title: Why governments arose
description: While humans were few there was hardly any government; in Sumer, sharing irrigation water called for a central authority. Today the UN has 193 member states.

facts.text: Britannica notes that so long as humans were few, there was hardly any government; the rise of agriculture began to change that.
In Sumer, in today's Iraq, irrigation farming meant the flow of water down the Tigris and Euphrates had to be coordinated by a central authority.
The United Nations has 193 member states, from large countries like India to small ones like Tuvalu.

title: Rules as a common code
description: Groups need shared rules so everyone plays the same game: in 1863 the Football Association was formed to set one definite code of football rules.

facts.text: Before the Football Association was formed in 1863, schools and clubs played football by their own rules, and there were 'feverish' disputes over how it should be played.
On 26 October 1863, clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London and formed the Football Association to establish a definite code of rules for the game.
FA founder Ebenezer Morley argued that football should have a set of rules in the same way that cricket had them.

title: Rules that coordinate: Sweden's Dagen H
description: Some rules matter because everyone follows the same one. Sweden drove on the left while its neighbors drove on the right, then switched to the right on 3 September 1967.

facts.text: Until 1967, Sweden drove on the left while its neighbors Denmark, Finland and Norway drove on the right, which led to accidents for Swedes abroad and visitors to Sweden.
On 3 September 1967, Dagen H, Sweden switched from left- to right-hand traffic: early that morning traffic stopped, then every vehicle moved to the right.

title: Power versus authority
description: Power is the ability to exercise your will over others; authority is power that people accept as legitimate and agree to follow.

facts.text: German sociologist Max Weber, in work published in 1922, defined power as the ability to exercise one's will over others.
Authority is accepted power: power that people agree to follow because they see it as legitimate.
For Weber, being obeyed is not enough for authority: the command must be accepted as valid.

title: Weber's three types of authority
description: Weber named three sources of legitimate authority: traditional (custom), charismatic (a leader's exceptional qualities) and legal-rational (laws and offices).

facts.text: Weber described three types of authority: traditional (long-standing custom), charismatic (a leader's exceptional personal qualities) and legal-rational (laws and written rules).
Examples: a monarch who inherits the throne holds traditional authority; Napoleon and Martin Luther King Jr. had charismatic authority; legal-rational authority resides in the office, not the person.

title: What makes a rule a law
description: A law is a rule of conduct that a community recognizes as binding, enforced through a controlling authority.

facts.text: Law is the set of rules of conduct that a community recognizes as binding, enforced through a controlling authority.

title: The Code of Hammurabi
description: Around 1750 BCE, Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 legal rulings engraved on a stone stela, written as if-then rules, including 'an eye for an eye'.

facts.text: Around 1750 BCE (about 3,800 years ago), Hammurabi of Babylon had 282 legal rulings engraved on a black stone stela more than 2.25 meters tall.
The stela of Hammurabi's code is now in the Louvre in Paris.
Hammurabi's laws follow an if-then pattern: if someone does something, then a set consequence follows.
Law 196 says that if a man puts out another man's eye, his eye shall be put out: an eye for an eye.
The code's epilogue invites anyone oppressed who has a case at law to come before the king's image and read the inscription.
Penalties in Hammurabi's code varied according to the social status of the offender and the circumstances.

title: Public services
description: Public services such as schools, transport, mail, police, fire and help for people in need are provided for everyone and paid for by taxes. In 2024, 1 in 4 people lacked safely managed drinking water.

facts.text: In 2024, about 2.1 billion people, 1 in 4 worldwide, still lacked safely managed drinking water, according to WHO and UNICEF.

Government provides public services such as public schools, public transportation, mail, police and fire departments, and food, housing and health care for the poor, usually available to all and paid for with taxes.

title: Public goods and free riders
description: Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival, like national defense; people can free ride on them, and taxes required by law overcome the free rider problem.

facts.text: A public good is nonexcludable (it is hard to stop anyone using it) and nonrival (one person's use doesn't leave less for others).
National defense is a classic public good: it protects everyone in the country, whether or not they paid.
Free riding means letting others pay for a public good while you enjoy it without paying.
When people agree through the political process to pay taxes, the law can require everyone to contribute, which overcomes the free rider problem.

title: What a tax is
description: The OECD defines taxes as compulsory, unrequited payments to government: what you get back isn't in proportion to what you paid. Taxes fall on income and profits, social security, payroll, property, and goods and services.

facts.text: The OECD defines taxes as compulsory, unrequited payments to government: unrequited because the benefits government provides are not normally in proportion to what each person pays.
The OECD classifies taxes by what they fall on: income and profits, social security contributions, payroll, property, and goods and services, such as value-added tax (VAT).

title: How much countries tax
description: In 2024, taxes averaged 34.1% of GDP across OECD countries, from 18.3% in Mexico to 45.2% in Denmark.

facts.text: In 2024, taxes averaged 34.1% of GDP across OECD countries, ranging from 18.3% in Mexico to 45.2% in Denmark, according to the OECD's Revenue Statistics 2025.
GDP measures the value of the final goods and services a country produces in a period, such as a year.

title: The social contract and Hobbes
description: A social contract is a real or imagined agreement setting out the rights and duties of rulers and ruled. Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651) said people give up freedom to a sovereign to escape a state of nature that is nasty, brutish and short.

facts.text: A social contract is an actual or hypothetical agreement between the ruled, or between rulers and ruled, setting out the rights and duties of each.
Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, after the English Civil War. Without government, he said, life would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short'.
For Hobbes, people escape the war of all against all by handing most of their freedom to an all-powerful sovereign in exchange for peace and protection.

title: Locke: rights and consent
description: Locke held that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property; government rests on consent, and people may resist a government that violates their rights.

facts.text: John Locke argued that even without government people have natural rights to life, liberty and property.
For Locke, government gets its legitimacy from the consent of the governed, and people may resist rulers who violate their rights.

title: Rousseau: the general will
description: Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762) opens 'Man was born free, and he is everywhere in chains' and grounds legitimate laws in the general will.

facts.text: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, born in Geneva, opened The Social Contract (1762) with: 'Man was born free, and he is everywhere in chains.'
Rousseau argued that legitimate laws come from the general will: people agree together to live by laws aimed at the common good, and obeying laws you make yourselves is a kind of freedom.

title: National, regional and local government
description: Many countries split government into layers. In Canada the federal level handles defence, foreign affairs, currency and passports; provinces and territories run education and health care; municipalities handle local services like waste, water and fire protection.

facts.text: Canada has three levels of government: federal, provincial or territorial, and municipal, each with its own responsibilities; some responsibilities are shared.
Canada's federal government is responsible for matters including national defence, foreign affairs, currency, citizenship and passports, criminal law and the postal service.
Canada's provinces and territories are responsible for education, colleges and universities, hospitals and health care, and social services.
Canada's municipal governments handle local services such as fire protection, local police, public transit, parks, waste management, water supply and local roads.

title: India's panchayats
description: India's 1992 73rd constitutional amendment made panchayats institutions of self-government at village, block and district levels, alongside the Union and state governments.

facts.text: India's 73rd constitutional amendment, passed in 1992, declared panchayats (elected councils) institutions of self-government alongside the Union and state governments.
India's panchayats work at three tiers: the village, the block and the district.

title: Nation versus state
description: A nation is a people with a shared identity; a state is a political organization with territory, laws and the means to enforce them. Their borders usually only partly overlap, as with the Kurds and the United Kingdom.

facts.text: A nation is a community sharing an identity, such as a culture, language or history; a state is a political organization with territory, laws and enforcement; a nation-state combines the two.
Britannica notes that the borders of states and the boundaries of nations usually only partly overlap.
The Kurds, estimated at 36 to 46 million in the mid-2010s, live mostly in parts of Iran, Iraq, Syria and Turkey, and have had no nation-state of their own in the modern era.
The United Kingdom is one state made up of four historical parts, England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each with its own customs and traditions.

title: Weber's definition of the state
description: Weber (1919) defined the state as a community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory.

facts.text: In 1919, Max Weber defined the state as a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.

title: Aristotle: humans as political animals
description: Aristotle held that humans are by nature political animals; the city-state comes into being for the sake of life but exists for the sake of the good life.

facts.text: Aristotle held that human beings are by nature political animals, and that anyone who cannot live in a community is either a beast or a god.
Aristotle wrote that the city-state comes into being for the sake of life but exists for the sake of the good life.

title: Monarchy: rule of one
description: A monarchy is the undivided rule of one person, the monarch, usually by heredity; Malaysia elects its paramount ruler for five years.

facts.text: The word monarchy comes from the Greek monarkhia, literally 'ruling of one', from monos (alone) and arkhein (to rule).
Britannica defines monarchy as a political system based on the undivided rule of a single person, the monarch, who is head of state and usually gets the position by heredity.
Britannica notes that successful and popular monarchs were believed to have a sacred right to rule.
Malaysia's head of state, the Yang di-Pertuan Agong ('paramount ruler'), is elected from among nine hereditary state rulers for a five-year term.

title: Absolute monarchy and divine right
description: Absolutism is unlimited central authority; Louis XIV (1643-1715) is the classic example, defended by the divine right of kings.

facts.text: Absolutism is unlimited, centralized authority held especially by a monarch or dictator.
Louis XIV of France, who reigned from 1643 to 1715, is Britannica's most familiar example of absolutism.
The divine right of kings, the most common defense of absolute monarchy, held that kings derived their authority from God.

title: Constitutional monarchy
description: A monarch shares power with a constitutional government and acts as a symbolic head of state: in Thiers's phrase, the king reigns but does not govern.

facts.text: Britannica defines constitutional monarchy as a system in which a monarch shares power with a constitutionally organized government, acting as a symbolic head of state.
Adolphe Thiers described a strictly symbolic monarch as one who 'reigns but does not govern'; France's Louis-Philippe, king from 1830, would not accept that role.
Britannica gives the United Kingdom, Belgium, Norway, Japan and Thailand as examples of constitutional monarchies.

title: Constitutional monarchy in Sweden and Japan
description: Sweden abolished royal absolutism in 1809 and made the King's role entirely ceremonial in 1974; Japan's Emperor is a symbol with no governmental powers.

facts.text: Sweden's 1809 Instrument of Government abolished royal absolutism; the King and the Riksdag, Sweden's parliament, were to share power.
Under Sweden's 1974 Instrument of Government, the King is still head of state but has no political power; his role is entirely ceremonial.
Japan's constitution makes the Emperor 'the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people' and gives him no powers related to government.

title: Dictatorship and how it keeps power
description: Dictatorship is absolute power without effective constitutional limits, gained by force or fraud and kept by terror and propaganda; the Roman dictator was a temporary crisis office.

facts.text: In the Roman Republic, a dictator was a temporary magistrate given extraordinary powers to deal with a state crisis.
A Roman dictator's term lasted at most six months.
Britannica notes that modern dictators resemble ancient tyrants rather than ancient Roman dictators.
Britannica defines dictatorship as government in which one person or a small group holds absolute power without effective constitutional limits.
Modern dictators typically gain power by force or fraud, keep it through intimidation, terror and suppressing civil liberties, and use mass propaganda to keep public support.

title: Totalitarianism
description: Totalitarian states seek control of every part of life; Mussolini coined the term, and Stalin's USSR and Nazi Germany are classic cases.

facts.text: Totalitarianism is government that permits no individual freedom and seeks to put every part of individual life under the authority of the state.
Benito Mussolini coined the term for Italy's fascist state: 'all within the state, none outside the state, none against the state'. Stalin's Soviet Union and Nazi Germany are other examples.

title: Oligarchy: rule by the few
description: Oligarchy is rule by a privileged few for their own ends, typically the wealthy; Aristotle set it against aristocracy, rule by the best.

facts.text: Oligarchy comes from the Greek oligos, 'few', and arkhein, 'to rule'.
Britannica defines oligarchy as government by the few, especially power used by a small privileged group for corrupt or selfish purposes.
Aristotle distinguished aristocracy, rule by the best, from oligarchy, rule by a few who serve themselves; in oligarchy the ruling few are typically the wealthy.

title: Venice's closed Great Council
description: Over about a century from 1297, Venice's Great Council closed to a fixed hereditary group, and the republic lasted into the late 18th century.

facts.text: Over about a century from 1297, Venice's Great Council, where sovereignty lay, was closed to all but a fixed hereditary group; from the 1390s new admissions ceased.
Venice's doge had immense prestige but was increasingly bound by his councils, and the Venetian constitution lasted into the late 18th century.

title: Michels's iron law of oligarchy
description: Robert Michels argued that every organization, even a democratic one, ends up ruled by an elite few.

facts.text: In the early 20th century, sociologist Robert Michels argued that every organization, even one committed to democratic ideals, ends up ruled by an elite few: the iron law of oligarchy.
Michels argued that leaders gain expertise, central authority and control of the bureaucracy and resources, which lets them dominate the members.

title: Theocracy: rule by religion
description: Theocracy is government by divine guidance or divinely guided officials, often clergy applying religious law.

facts.text: Theocracy comes from the Greek theokratia, 'rule of God', a word attributed to the historian Josephus.
Britannica defines theocracy as government by divine guidance or by officials regarded as divinely guided; often leaders are clergy and the law is based on religious law.
Britannica names Saudi Arabia, Iran and the Vatican as contemporary theocracies.

title: Theocracy today: the Vatican and Iran
description: The pope, elected by cardinals, holds all three powers in Vatican City; Iran's supreme leader, a jurist chosen by an elected assembly, stands above an elected president.

facts.text: Vatican City, at 0.44 square kilometers the world's smallest fully independent state, is led by the pope, who holds absolute executive, legislative and judicial powers there.
The pope is elected in the Sistine Chapel by cardinals under 80, needing a two-thirds majority; black smoke means no decision, white smoke a new pope.
Since 1979, Iran's head of state has been a supreme leader, a jurist of Islamic law chosen by the Assembly of Experts, a body of Islamic jurists directly elected every eight years.
Iran's president and legislature are directly elected, but the supreme leader can approve or dismiss the president and commands the armed forces.

title: Direct democracy
description: In direct democracy citizens decide issues themselves rather than electing representatives; it is hard to run at the scale of a large state.

facts.text: In direct democracy, citizens make decisions themselves, often voting on issues; in representative democracy, they elect officials to decide for them.
Britannica notes the argument that direct democracy cannot work across large modern states; today it mostly works as specific tools inside representative systems.

title: Assemblies of citizens
description: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden's Landsgemeinde and New England town meetings let voters decide in person.

facts.text: In the Swiss cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden, voters gather once a year in an open-air assembly, the Landsgemeinde, and vote on laws and taxes by a show of hands.
Critics of the Landsgemeinde complained that a secret ballot is impossible in it.
A New England town meeting is an assembly of a town's qualified voters, who elect officials and school boards and debate and vote on taxes and spending.

title: Republics
description: A republic, from res publica, 'the public thing', is ruled by representatives of the citizens and has no hereditary monarch; Rome's began in 509 BCE.

facts.text: The Roman Republic began in 509 BCE, when the Romans replaced their monarchy with elected magistrates, led by two consuls elected every year.
The word republic comes from the Latin res publica, 'the public thing', which once covered any non-tyrannical state, including oligarchies.
Britannica defines a republic as a state ruled by representatives of the citizen body; the word is used for any government whose head of state is not a hereditary monarch.
Sweden replaced its 1809 Instrument of Government in 1974 because it had become a parliamentary democracy while the old text still had the King ruling.

title: Madison's case for representation
description: In Federalist No. 10, Madison argued that delegating government to elected representatives lets a republic span more citizens and territory than a pure democracy.

facts.text: In Federalist No. 10 (1787), James Madison said a republic differs from a pure democracy by delegating government to a small number of citizens elected by the rest, so it can span more citizens and territory.
Madison hoped representatives would 'refine and enlarge the public views' by passing them through a chosen body of citizens.

title: Federal systems
description: Federalism divides power between the center and the regions under a constitution that neither can change alone.

facts.text: Federalism unites separate states or regions in one system while each keeps its own integrity, usually under a written constitution that can be changed only by extraordinary procedures.
The United States, Switzerland, Canada, Australia, Germany, India and Brazil are federal countries.

title: Unitary systems
description: In a unitary state the center holds the power and delegates it; the UK devolves power to Scotland but its Parliament remains sovereign.

facts.text: In a unitary state, most or all governing power sits with the central government, which delegates authority to regional and local units.
Britannica calls France the classic example of a centralized administrative system.
Inside the federal United States, each state is itself a unitary government: its counties and cities are created by state law.
The Scottish Parliament, set up by the UK Parliament's Scotland Act 1998, opened in 1999; the UK Parliament can still legislate for all parts of the UK, including devolved areas.
Britannica says Britain decentralizes power in practice though not in constitutional principle.

title: Failed and fragile states
description: A failed state loses control of its territory and the monopoly of legitimate force and provides only minimal services; the Fragile States Index tracks the pressures.

facts.text: Britannica describes a failed state as one that cannot project authority over its territory and people or protect its borders, cannot keep a monopoly on the legitimate use of violence, and provides only minimal public services.
Britannica lists symptoms of failed states: crumbling infrastructure, flourishing corruption, and worsening basic measures such as infant mortality and literacy.
The Fund for Peace's Fragile States Index scores countries on twelve indicators, including state legitimacy, public services, and refugees and internally displaced people.

title: Somalia's collapse
description: After Siad Barre's overthrow in 1991, Somalia descended into state collapse under rival warlords and decades of civil war.

facts.text: In 1991 Somalia's president, Mohamed Siad Barre, was overthrown in a popular uprising, and the country descended into state collapse under rival warlords.
Somalia's 1991 collapse was followed by more than three decades of civil war.

title: Aristotle's six forms of government
description: Aristotle classified constitutions by who rules (one, few, many) and whether they serve the common advantage or the rulers' own.

facts.text: Aristotle sorted constitutions by who rules (one, few or many) and whether they aim at the common advantage (kingship, aristocracy, polity) or the rulers' own (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy).
In Aristotle's scheme, 'democracy' meant rule by the poor in their own interest, as oligarchy was rule by the wealthy in theirs.

title: Democracy's Athenian roots
description: Democracy is Greek for rule by the people. In Athens, Cleisthenes' reforms (508-507 BCE) based political rights on the local deme, but only free adult male citizens took part.

facts.text: The word democracy comes from the Greek demokratia, coined in the middle of the 5th century BCE (about 2,500 years ago) from demos, 'people', and kratos, 'rule'.
Cleisthenes, regarded as the founder of Athenian democracy, had his reforms approved in 508-507 BCE; they based political rights on membership of a deme, or township, instead of family or clan.
Cleisthenes replaced Athens' four kinship-based tribes with ten new local tribes.
Athenian democracy included only a minority: free adult male citizens. Women, enslaved people and resident foreigners were excluded.

title: Of, by and for the people
description: At Gettysburg on 19 November 1863, Lincoln resolved that government of the people, by the people, for the people shall not perish from the earth.

facts.text: On 19 November 1863, dedicating a national cemetery for Union soldiers at Gettysburg, Abraham Lincoln resolved that 'government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.'

title: Magna Carta: the king under the law
description: On 15 June 1215 at Runnymede, King John agreed to Magna Carta under pressure from rebel barons. Its 63 clauses established that the sovereign is subject to the rule of law.

facts.text: On 15 June 1215, at Runnymede beside the River Thames, King John agreed to Magna Carta, Latin for 'Great Charter', under pressure from rebellious barons.
The 1215 Magna Carta contained 63 clauses.
Britannica says Magna Carta established the principle that the sovereign is subject to the rule of law, and documented the liberties held by 'free men'.

title: Magna Carta's key clauses
description: Clause 39: no imprisonment without lawful judgment. Clause 40: justice not sold, denied or delayed. Clause 12: no scutage or aid without general consent. Clause 61: 25 barons could enforce it.

facts.text: Clause 39: no free man shall be seized or imprisoned, stripped of his rights or possessions, outlawed or exiled, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.
Clause 40: 'To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice.'
Clause 12: no 'scutage' or 'aid', payments the king demanded, could be levied without the kingdom's general consent, apart from three customary cases such as ransoming the king.
Clause 61 had the barons choose 25 of their number to enforce the charter; if the king broke it, they could seize his castles, lands and possessions until he made amends.

title: Parliaments: old roots, one or two chambers
description: Parliament means a place for talking. Iceland's Althing, founded around 930, is one of the oldest national parliaments and has one chamber; the UK Parliament has two, the elected Commons and the mainly appointed Lords.

facts.text: Iceland's Althing, founded at Thingvellir around 930 and meeting there until 1798, is one of the oldest national parliaments in the world.
Iceland's Althing is a unicameral legislature: it has a single chamber.
The word parliament comes from Old French parlement, 'a speaking, talk', from parler, 'to speak'.
The UK Parliament is bicameral: an elected House of Commons and a House of Lords whose members are mainly appointed.

title: What a parliament does
description: A parliament makes laws, controls taxes and spending, and holds the government to account. In the UK, the Commons alone imposes taxes and a prime minister needs its majority.

facts.text: The main function of the UK Parliament is to legislate: to make laws.
The UK House of Commons has the sole right to impose taxes and to allocate funds to government departments and services.
A UK prime minister must keep the support of a majority in the House of Commons to stay in office, and government decisions face scrutiny and debate in Parliament.

title: Parliamentary and presidential systems
description: In a parliamentary system the legislature selects the prime minister; in a presidential system the president is elected to a fixed term and is also head of state. France is semi-presidential.

facts.text: In a parliamentary system the head of government, the prime minister, is selected by the legislature; usually the party or coalition with the most seats forms the government.
In a presidential system the head of government is popularly elected to a fixed term, does not depend on the legislature for power, and is also head of state; the United States is an example.
Head of state is a ceremonial role; head of government is a political role with real power. In parliamentary systems they are separate, as with Germany's president and chancellor.
The UK, Germany, India and Japan have parliamentary systems. France is semi-presidential: an elected president and a prime minister chosen by the legislature both wield power.

title: Losing the confidence of parliament
description: A prime minister can be removed whenever they lose the confidence of a majority of parliament. On 28 March 1979 the Callaghan government lost a no-confidence vote 311 to 310.

facts.text: In a parliamentary system, a prime minister can be removed from power whenever they lose the confidence of a majority of parliament.
On 28 March 1979 the House of Commons passed a motion of no confidence in James Callaghan's government by 311 votes to 310, and Callaghan asked for a general election.

title: Separation of powers
description: Separation of powers divides legislative, executive and judicial functions among separate bodies. Montesquieu (1748) warned that power tends to be abused and there is no liberty when the powers are united.

facts.text: Separation of powers is the division of government's legislative, executive and judicial functions among separate and independent bodies, to limit arbitrary excesses by government.
In The Spirit of Laws (1748), Montesquieu wrote that every man invested with power is apt to abuse it, and to carry his authority as far as it will go.
Montesquieu wrote that when the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body there can be no liberty, and no liberty if the judicial power is not separated from them.

title: Bagehot's fusion of powers
description: Walter Bagehot (The English Constitution, 1867) called the efficient secret of Britain's system the nearly complete fusion of executive and legislative powers, linked by the Cabinet.

facts.text: In The English Constitution (1867), Walter Bagehot called the 'efficient secret' of Britain's system the close union, the nearly complete fusion, of the executive and legislative powers.
Bagehot wrote that the connecting link is the Cabinet: a committee of the legislative body selected to be the executive body.

title: Checks and balances
description: Checks and balances empower each branch to block actions by the others. Montesquieu: power should be a check to power. The Federalist No. 51: if men were angels, no government would be necessary.

facts.text: The Federalist No. 51 (1788), generally credited to James Madison, says: 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.'
The Federalist No. 51 also says: 'Ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'
Checks and balances is the principle under which separate branches of government are empowered to prevent actions by other branches and are induced to share power.
Montesquieu wrote that 'power should be a check to power'.

Examples of checks: only the US Congress can appropriate funds; a parliament can pass a no-confidence vote, and in many parliamentary systems the government can call an early election; courts review whether government actions are constitutional.

title: A check in action: South Korea 2016-2017
description: South Korea's National Assembly impeached President Park Geun-hye on 9 December 2016; the Constitutional Court unanimously upheld it on 10 March 2017, removing her from office.

facts.text: On 9 December 2016, South Korea's National Assembly voted by an overwhelming margin to impeach President Park Geun-hye.
On 10 March 2017 South Korea's Constitutional Court unanimously upheld the impeachment, and Park became the first democratically elected South Korean president removed from office.

title: What political parties are and do
description: A political party is a group organized to acquire and exercise political power. Parties recruit candidates, organize voters, form governments and provide opposition, though Washington warned against the spirit of party in 1796.

facts.text: In his Farewell Address of 1796, George Washington warned against 'the baneful effects of the spirit of party'.
Political parties took their modern form in Europe and the United States in the 19th century.
Britannica defines a political party as a group of persons organized to acquire and exercise political power.
Parties recruit candidates, organize voters at elections, form and keep governments going, and give those out of power an organized opposition.

title: Whig and Tory: insults turned names
description: Britain's first party names began as terms of abuse in 1679: Tory meant an Irish outlaw, and Whig probably came from a Scottish word for a horse drover.

facts.text: 'Whig' and 'Tory' began as terms of abuse in 1679, during the struggle over excluding James, Duke of York, from the throne, and were later adopted by the parties themselves.
'Tory' first meant an Irish outlaw or robber; 'Whig' probably came from a Scottish word for a horse drover.

title: Sweden's 1766 press freedom law
description: On 2 December 1766 Sweden's Riksdag passed what is regarded as the world's first law for press freedom and freedom of information, abolishing censorship and opening government documents.

facts.text: On 2 December 1766, Sweden's parliament, the Riksdag, passed what is regarded as the world's first law supporting freedom of the press and freedom of information.
Sweden's 1766 act abolished censorship of printed publications, including imports but not academic and theological works, and guaranteed public access to government documents.

title: Why a free press matters
description: Press freedom is the right to report news without government control, giving citizens informed access to political information. Carlyle called the press gallery a Fourth Estate.

facts.text: Freedom of the press is the right of media outlets to report news without government control; it permits informed access to information and opinions about political matters.

Thomas Carlyle wrote that Burke said there were Three Estates in Parliament, 'but, in the Reporters' Gallery yonder, there sat a Fourth Estate more important far than they all.' The press is still called the Fourth Estate.

title: Speakers' Corner
description: At Speakers' Corner in Hyde Park anyone may speak on any subject if it is lawful. After an 1866 protest broke down the park railings, an 1872 act set rules for meeting and speaking there.

facts.text: At Speakers' Corner in London's Hyde Park, anyone can turn up unannounced and speak on any subject, as long as the police consider the speech lawful.
In 1866 the government suppressed a Reform League meeting in Hyde Park that demanded a wider right to vote; finding the park locked, demonstrators tore up hundreds of yards of railings.
The Parks Regulation Act of 1872 set out rules under which people could meet and speak freely in Hyde Park.

title: Expression and assembly in international law
description: The UN's International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) protects opinion and expression (Article 19) and peaceful assembly (Article 21), with limits only by law where necessary.

facts.text: The UN General Assembly adopted the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights on 16 December 1966.
Article 19 of the Covenant: everyone has the right to hold opinions without interference, and to freedom of expression, including to seek, receive and impart information and ideas of all kinds.
Article 21 of the Covenant: 'The right of peaceful assembly shall be recognized.'

Under the Covenant, expression and assembly may be restricted only by law and where necessary, for example to respect the rights or reputations of others or to protect national security, public order, or public health or morals.

title: Churchill's 'worst form of government'
description: On 11 November 1947 Churchill told the Commons that no one pretends democracy is perfect, and that 'it has been said' democracy is the worst form of government except all the others tried.

facts.text: On 11 November 1947, Winston Churchill told the House of Commons: 'it has been said that democracy is the worst form of Government except all those other forms that have been tried from time to time.'
In the same remarks Churchill said no one pretends democracy is perfect or all-wise, and his words 'it has been said' show he was repeating an existing saying, not coining it.

title: What a constitution is
description: A constitution is a state's fundamental organizing principle and supreme law: it sets up the system of government, distributes and constrains power, and protects rights. Aristotle called it the arrangement of the offices.

facts.text: A constitution is the body of doctrines and practices that form the fundamental organizing principle of a political state.
International IDEA describes a constitution as the supreme law of a country; day-to-day political decisions and ordinary laws are made within its framework.
Constitutions establish the system of government, distribute and constrain power, and protect the rights of citizens.
Britannica traces the idea of a constitution to the ancient Greeks, especially Aristotle, whose simplest definition was 'the arrangement of the offices in a polis' (state).

title: Written and unwritten constitutions
description: Some constitutions, like the US one, are a single written document; the UK's is a collection of documents, statutes and practices. Nearly every state claims a constitution, but not all follow theirs.

facts.text: In the United States the constitution is a specific written document; in the United Kingdom it is a collection of documents, statutes and traditional practices generally accepted as governing political matters.
Britannica notes that virtually every state claims to have a constitution, but not every government conducts itself in a consistently constitutional manner.

title: The U.S. Constitution
description: Signed in Philadelphia on 17 September 1787 to replace the Articles of Confederation, the U.S. Constitution took effect in 1789 and is the oldest written national constitution in use. It opens 'We the People'.

facts.text: Britannica describes the U.S. Constitution as the oldest written national constitution in use.
All four pages of the original U.S. Constitution are on permanent display at the National Archives.
The U.S. Constitution was drafted in Philadelphia in the summer of 1787 and signed by 39 delegates on 17 September 1787.
It replaced the Articles of Confederation, which had denied the national government essential powers such as direct taxation and regulating commerce between the states.
Article VII required ratification by nine states; after nine ratified, the Constitution took effect in 1789.
The Preamble begins 'We the People of the United States' and says they 'do ordain and establish this Constitution for the United States of America'.

title: Inside the U.S. Constitution
description: Its seven articles set up Congress, the President and the courts, and Article VI makes it 'the supreme Law of the Land'. The first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, are the Bill of Rights.

facts.text: The U.S. Constitution has seven articles; Article I vests lawmaking power in Congress, Article II executive power in a President, Article III judicial power in a Supreme Court and lower courts.
Article VI says the Constitution and the laws made in pursuance of it 'shall be the supreme Law of the Land'.
The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1791, are known as the Bill of Rights.
The First Amendment begins: 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof', and protects speech, the press, assembly and petition.

title: How constitutions are amended
description: Most constitutions make amending harder than ordinary lawmaking (supermajorities, referendums, double decisions, approval by states) to balance flexibility against protection; some provisions cannot be amended at all.

facts.text: Most constitutions make amending harder than passing ordinary laws, using a legislative supermajority, a referendum, a double decision (sometimes with an intervening election) or approval by states or regions.
An amendment process that is too rigid prevents necessary reforms; one that is too flexible leaves a constitution's rights and institutions vulnerable to erosion by the government in power.
Under Article V, a U.S. amendment is proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or by a convention) and must be ratified by three-fourths of the states.
The U.S. Constitution has been amended 27 times.
Some countries require a referendum for every constitutional amendment, however small, including Australia, Denmark, Ireland and Japan.
In Ireland, an amendment is passed by parliament in the same way as an ordinary law and then needs approval by a majority of votes cast in a referendum.
More than 70 constitutions have provisions that cannot be amended, such as basic human rights in Germany; these are often the result of past traumas like conflict or dictatorship.

title: The 27th Amendment and Gregory Watson
description: A congressional pay amendment proposed in 1789 was ratified in 1992 after a campaign begun by a student, Gregory Watson, whose 1982 paper arguing it was still pending got a C.

facts.text: The 27th Amendment, which delays changes to congressional pay until after the next House election, was proposed on 25 September 1789 and ratified on 7 May 1992.

In 1982 Gregory Watson, a University of Texas at Austin sophomore, got a C for a paper arguing the pay amendment was still pending because no deadline was set; he campaigned for ratification, and in 2017 the grade became an A.

title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
description: The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948, with no votes against. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired its drafting.

facts.text: The UN General Assembly proclaimed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris on 10 December 1948 (resolution 217 A).
The Declaration was adopted with eight countries abstaining and none voting against.

Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting; France's René Cassin wrote the first draft, with Lebanon's Charles Malik and China's Peng Chung Chang; the Commission's 18 members came from various political, cultural and religious backgrounds.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is available in more than 500 languages.

title: What the Declaration says
description: Its 30 articles begin 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights', apply without distinction of any kind, and promise life, liberty and security of person.

facts.text: The Declaration has 30 articles. Article 1: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.' Article 2: its rights belong to everyone without distinction of race, colour, sex, language, religion or opinion.
Article 3 of the Declaration says: 'Everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of person.'

title: From declaration to law
description: The Declaration was proclaimed as a common standard and was not binding, which was first seen as a weakness; two covenants followed in 1966, and many countries wrote it into their constitutions.

facts.text: The UN proclaimed the Declaration as a common standard of achievement for all peoples and nations; Britannica notes its nonbinding status was first seen as a major weakness.
In 1966 the UN adopted the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
The Declaration has inspired more than seventy human rights treaties, and many countries have incorporated it into their national constitutions.

title: Freedom of religion: belief and practice
description: Everyone may hold, adopt or change a religion or belief, and no limits on belief are allowed; showing it in practice may be limited, but only by law and where necessary for safety, order, health, morals or others' rights.

facts.text: Article 18 of the Universal Declaration gives everyone freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including freedom to change religion or belief and to manifest it in teaching, practice, worship and observance.
The UN Human Rights Committee says no limitations are permitted on the freedom to have or adopt a religion or belief of one's choice, and the ICCPR bars coercion that would impair it.

Under ICCPR Article 18(3), freedom to manifest religion or belief may be limited only by law and where necessary to protect public safety, order, health, morals or others' fundamental rights and freedoms.

title: Religion and the state
description: Countries arrange religion and state differently: the US bars Congress from establishing a religion, France's 1905 law separated churches and state, and England has an established church with the monarch as supreme governor.

facts.text: France's 1905 law separated churches and the state, barring the state from officially recognizing, funding or endorsing religious groups.
The Church of England is the established church of England, and the British monarch is its supreme governor.

title: Debate: France's 2004 school symbols law
description: France's 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols for public school pupils. The Stasi Commission and President Chirac backed it as secularism; Human Rights Watch called it an unwarranted infringement on religious practice.

facts.text: On 15 March 2004 France banned public school pupils from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, such as Muslim headscarves, Sikh turbans, Jewish skullcaps and large Christian crosses.
The Stasi Commission recommended the ban and President Jacques Chirac backed it as applying laïcité, France's principle of secularism.
Human Rights Watch called the proposed law an unwarranted infringement on the right to religious practice, arguing such symbols threatened no one's safety, order or rights.

title: The right to privacy
description: Warren and Brandeis (1890) called privacy 'the right to be let alone'. The Universal Declaration's Article 12 protects it; the US Constitution never names it, but courts built it from amendments such as the Fourth.

facts.text: In an 1890 Harvard Law Review article, Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis described the right to privacy as 'the right to be let alone'.
Warren and Brandeis wrote that 'instantaneous photographs and newspaper enterprise have invaded the sacred precincts of private and domestic life'.
Article 12 of the Universal Declaration: no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with their privacy, family, home or correspondence, nor to attacks upon their honour and reputation.
The U.S. Constitution has no explicit privacy clause; courts have drawn privacy protections from the First, Fourth and Fifth Amendments, and in 1965 the Supreme Court described a 'zone of privacy'.
The Fourth Amendment protects people 'in their persons, houses, papers, and effects' against unreasonable searches and seizures, and requires warrants based on probable cause.

title: Data protection and its limits
description: In the EU, data protection is a fundamental right and the GDPR has applied since 25 May 2018, with rights to see and erase your data. Privacy is balanced against free expression and national security.

facts.text: In the EU, data protection is a fundamental right under Article 8 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has applied since 25 May 2018.

Under EU rules you can ask an organisation whether it holds your personal data and, in some cases, have it erased (the 'right to be forgotten'); erasure does not apply where processing is needed for freedom of expression, a legal obligation or legal claims.
Britannica cites the 2001 USA PATRIOT Act, which expanded federal access to business records in terrorism investigations, as an example of tension between privacy and national security.

title: Suffrage and who had it
description: Suffrage is the right to vote. In 18th- and 19th-century Britain it required property ('a stake in the country'), and some countries once excluded voters by race.

facts.text: Britannica defines suffrage as the right to vote in electing public officials and in adopting or rejecting proposed legislation.
In 18th- and 19th-century Britain voters needed a property or income qualification, on the argument that only those with a stake in the country should have a voice in its affairs.
Some countries have limited the vote by race: South Africa at one time, and the Old South of the United States, did not permit their Black populations to vote.

title: Voting amendments in the U.S. Constitution
description: Amendments widened the U.S. vote: the 15th (1870) on race, the 24th (1964) against poll taxes, the 26th (1971) for citizens 18 and over.

facts.text: The 15th Amendment, ratified in 1870, says the vote shall not be denied or abridged on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.
The 24th Amendment, ratified in 1964, bars denying the vote in federal elections for failure to pay a poll tax.
The 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971, bars denying the vote on account of age to citizens who are 18 or older.

title: Universal suffrage
description: The Universal Declaration's Article 21 makes the will of the people, expressed in genuine elections by universal and equal suffrage, the basis of government's authority. The line keeps moving: Austria votes at 16.

facts.text: Article 21 of the Universal Declaration: the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections by universal and equal suffrage and secret vote.
Austria's 2007 electoral reform lowered its voting age from 18 to 16, making it the first country in Europe to do so for all citizens.

title: New Zealand: women vote first
description: On 19 September 1893 New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in parliamentary elections, after Kate Sheppard's campaign and a petition of 31,872 signatures.

facts.text: On 19 September 1893 New Zealand women were granted the vote, making New Zealand the first self-governing country to give women the vote in parliamentary elections.

Kate Sheppard of the Women's Christian Temperance Union led a seven-year campaign; in 1893 its 13 petitions gathered 31,872 signatures, the largest in Australasia, and the main one was reportedly carried to Parliament in a wheelbarrow.

title: Britain: suffragists and suffragettes
description: British suffragists, led by Millicent Fawcett, used law-abiding methods; suffragettes, led by the Pankhursts, used radical action. Women over 30 first voted in 1918; equal votes at 21 came in 1928.

facts.text: The National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, formed in 1897 and led by Millicent Fawcett, used law-abiding tactics: lobbying Parliament, peaceful marches, petitions and public meetings.

The suffragettes, led by Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst, believed only radical action would force a change in the law; their 1906 to 1914 campaign escalated to window-smashing and fires, and many went to prison.
In 1918 over 8 million British women over 30 voted in a general election for the first time; in 1928 every man and woman over 21 got the vote on equal terms.

title: Women's suffrage in the U.S. and Switzerland
description: The 19th Amendment (1920) bars denying the vote on account of sex. Swiss men voted down women's suffrage in 1959; Swiss women won the federal vote in 1971.

facts.text: The 19th Amendment, ratified on 18 August 1920, bars denying the vote on account of sex.
Swiss voters, all men, rejected women's suffrage on 1 February 1959; on 7 February 1971 Swiss women won the right to vote and stand for election.

title: What civil rights are
description: Civil rights are guarantees of equal opportunity and equal protection under the law regardless of race, religion or other characteristics; unlike civil liberties (restraints on government), they usually need positive government action.

facts.text: Britannica defines civil rights as guarantees of equal social opportunities and equal protection under the law, regardless of race, religion or other personal characteristics.
Britannica contrasts civil liberties, freedoms secured by placing restraints on government, with civil rights, which require positive government action, often legislation.

title: The U.S. civil rights movement
description: Rosa Parks's 1955 arrest sparked the Montgomery bus boycott; courts struck down bus segregation; the Civil Rights Act (1964) banned discrimination and the Voting Rights Act (1965) outlawed literacy tests.

facts.text: On 1 December 1955 Rosa Parks, 43, was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger; the bus boycott that followed lasted about a year, and Martin Luther King Jr. was elected to lead its organisers.
A federal district court found segregation on publicly operated buses unconstitutional, and the U.S. Supreme Court affirmed the ruling.
On 2 July 1964 President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act, which banned discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin in public accommodations and employment.
The Voting Rights Act, signed on 6 August 1965, outlawed literacy tests as a prerequisite to voting; it enforced the 15th Amendment, 95 years after that amendment's ratification.
An attack by state troopers on peaceful marchers in Selma, Alabama, gained national attention and helped persuade President Johnson and Congress to pass voting rights legislation.

title: The end of apartheid
description: Apartheid ('apartness'), set up in South Africa in 1948, classified people by race and used pass laws; it was repealed in the early 1990s, and the 1994 elections brought a government led by Nelson Mandela.

facts.text: Apartheid, Afrikaans for 'apartness', was formally established in South Africa in 1948; its laws classified people by race, and pass laws required nonwhite people to carry documents to be in restricted areas.
Apartheid legislation was repealed in the early 1990s under President F. W. de Klerk, and the 1994 elections produced a government led by Nelson Mandela.

title: South Africa's 1996 Constitution
description: Mandela signed South Africa's constitution at Sharpeville on 10 December 1996, Human Rights Day. It is the supreme law, and its Bill of Rights protects equality, religion, privacy and the vote.

facts.text: On 21 March 1960 police opened fire on a crowd demonstrating against pass laws at Sharpeville, South Africa.
President Nelson Mandela signed South Africa's constitution into law at Sharpeville on 10 December 1996, International Human Rights Day.
South Africa's 1996 Constitution is a single written document of 14 chapters; Chapter 2 is the Bill of Rights.
Section 2 says the Constitution is the supreme law of the Republic; law or conduct inconsistent with it is invalid.
Section 7(1) calls the Bill of Rights 'a cornerstone of democracy in South Africa' that enshrines the rights of all people and affirms human dignity, equality and freedom.

South Africa's Bill of Rights bans unfair discrimination on grounds including race, sex, religion, age and disability, and protects privacy, freedom of religion and belief, and every adult citizen's vote by secret ballot.

title: What a bill is
description: A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing one; once both Houses agree and it receives Royal Assent, it becomes an Act.

facts.text: In the UK Parliament, a bill is a proposal for a new law, or to change an existing law, presented for debate; after Royal Assent it becomes an Act of Parliament and is law.

title: The stages of a bill
description: A UK bill passes first reading, second reading, committee, report and third reading in each House, with ping-pong until both agree its exact wording; a US bill must pass both chambers in identical form.

facts.text: In the UK House of Commons, first reading is a formality without debate: the bill's short title is read out and it is ordered to be printed.

After first reading, a UK bill goes through second reading (a debate on its general principles), committee stage (line-by-line examination), report stage and third reading, then the same stages in the other House, before Royal Assent.
Both Houses of the UK Parliament must agree the exact wording of a bill; if they disagree, it passes back and forth between them, nicknamed ping-pong, before Royal Assent.
In the United States, a bill must be passed by both the House and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the President to be signed into law.

title: How lawmakers debate
description: Debate on a bill's principles happens at second reading, under rules that keep it about ideas: no names, and no accusations of lying.

facts.text: In the UK House of Commons, members may not refer to each other by name in debate, to guard against personality in debate; they use forms such as "the honourable Member for" a constituency.
At second reading, the UK House of Commons debates the general principles of a bill.
Alleging that another member has lied is almost always out of order in the Commons; the Speaker directs a member who uses unparliamentary language to withdraw it, and refusing can lead to suspension.

title: The filibuster and cloture
description: The US Senate allows extended debate, so long speeches can delay a bill (a filibuster); cloture ends debate, by two-thirds from 1917 and three-fifths since 1975.

facts.text: The word filibuster comes from a Dutch word for "freebooter" and the Spanish "filibusteros", names for pirates raiding Caribbean islands.
In the US Senate, the right of extended debate lets senators use long speeches to delay action on a bill: a filibuster.
In 1917 the US Senate adopted a cloture rule to end debate by a two-thirds vote; in 1975 it lowered the bar to three-fifths of senators, usually 60 of 100.

title: Committees and bills
description: Most detailed lawmaking happens in committees: bills are referred to them, most die there, and the rest go through hearings and mark-up.

facts.text: In his 1885 book Congressional Government, Woodrow Wilson wrote that "Congress in session is Congress on public exhibition, whilst Congress in its committee-rooms is Congress at work."
Bills in the US House are referred to committees, each with jurisdiction over an area of policy, such as agriculture or education.
Most bills in the US Congress die in committee: they are never reported out to the whole House or Senate.

A US House committee usually first holds a public hearing with witnesses representing various viewpoints, then a mark-up session to vote on amendments; it can then report the bill or table it, ending action.

title: Select committees
description: In the UK, a Commons select committee shadows each government department, examining its spending, policies and administration.

facts.text: The UK House of Commons has a select committee for each government department, examining its spending, policies and administration; committees can question ministers and officials in public.

title: What lobbying is
description: Lobbying is trying to influence government decisions; the word comes from the lobbies where people waited for lawmakers, and many kinds of groups do it.

facts.text: Lobbying is named after the lobbies outside legislative chambers where people seeking influence gathered; Britannica traces it to constituents meeting representatives in the lobby of England's House of Commons in the 17th century.
Lobbying is the practice by individuals, organizations or interest groups of trying to influence government decisions and public policy.

Those who lobby include businesses, trade associations, labor unions, charities and other nonprofits, universities, religious organizations, local governments and citizen groups; individuals lobby when they contact lawmakers about legislation.

title: The debate over lobbying and its regulation
description: Supporters say lobbying brings expertise and voice; critics say it can make influence unequal. Governments respond mainly with registration and disclosure.

facts.text: The OECD says lobbying can give policy makers valuable insights and data for better-informed policies, but abuse, such as special interests monopolizing influence, can lead to worse policies.
Supporters see lobbying as central to representative democracy; critics argue it can entrench access for elites, making influence unequal.
In 2010 the OECD adopted the first international standard on transparency and integrity in lobbying.
The US Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 requires lobbyists to register with the Clerk of the House and the Secretary of the Senate and to report on their lobbying.
Since 1 July 2021, EU rules make registration in a transparency register a condition for lobbyists to carry out activities such as meeting Commissioners and EU officials.

title: What a veto is
description: A veto is an executive's power to reject a bill; the word is Latin for "I forbid", from the protests of Rome's tribunes.

facts.text: Veto is Latin for "I forbid"; in ancient Rome it was the term for a protest by a tribune of the people against a measure of the Senate or the magistrates.
In government, a veto is an executive's power to reject a bill, preventing it from becoming law.

title: The US veto and override
description: The US President has 10 days (Sundays excepted) to sign or veto a bill; Congress can override by two-thirds of each chamber, but not a pocket veto.

facts.text: Under the US Constitution, the President has 10 days (Sundays excepted) to sign a bill or veto it by returning it to Congress with objections; Congress can override by a two-thirds vote in each chamber.
If Congress adjourns so that the President cannot return a bill within the 10 days, the bill is pocket vetoed, and Congress cannot override a pocket veto.
Franklin D. Roosevelt vetoed 635 bills, more than any other US president, and Congress overrode 9 of them.

title: Veto overrides around the world
description: Override thresholds vary: two-thirds is most common, Poland needs three-fifths and Brazil an absolute majority; a veto changes the majority a bill needs.

facts.text: Veto override rules vary: two-thirds is most common (for example Mexico, Ghana and the Philippines), Poland requires three-fifths, and Brazil an absolute majority in both chambers.
International IDEA notes that a veto lets a president change the majority a bill needs: an ordinary majority if the president supports it, a supermajority if the president opposes it.

title: Secondary legislation
description: In the UK, ministers make secondary legislation, mostly statutory instruments, under powers in an Act, to fill in its details.

facts.text: In the UK, secondary legislation is law made by ministers or other bodies under powers given to them by an Act of Parliament; it fills in the details needed to make Acts work in practice.
About 3,500 statutory instruments, the most common form of UK secondary legislation, are made each year; only about 1,000 need to be considered by Parliament.

title: US rulemaking
description: US agencies write regulations under authority from laws enacted by Congress, through an open notice-and-comment process that is not a vote.

facts.text: US agencies get their authority to issue regulations from laws enacted by Congress, and must not act beyond that authority.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act of 1946, a US agency publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register, takes public comments, then publishes a final rule, which goes into the Code of Federal Regulations.
Anyone can comment on a proposed US federal rule, but it is not a vote: an agency may not base its final rule on the number of comments for or against, and must reason from the record.
The US Environmental Protection Agency advises that one well-supported comment is often more informative to it than a thousand form letters.

title: Byelaws: local laws
description: A byelaw is a local law made by a local authority for its own area, using powers granted by Acts of Parliament.

facts.text: Leeds City Council's byelaws cover subjects including hairdressers and barbers, ear piercing, pleasure fairs, the employment of children and the city's parks.
Byelaws are local laws made by a local authority that apply only within a specific area, made using powers granted by Acts of Parliament.

title: Where local lawmaking power comes from
description: Local governments can make only the laws a higher government allows: Canada's municipalities are "creatures" of the provinces, and US states follow Dillon's Rule or home rule.

facts.text: Canada's Constitution Act, 1867 gives provinces power over municipal institutions; courts have called municipalities "creatures" of the provincial legislature, with only the powers provincial law confers.
Under Dillon's Rule, from two 1868 decisions by Iowa judge John F. Dillon, a US local government may act only where the state has granted it the power, expressly or by clear implication.
Home rule, which emerged in the early 1900s, delegates broader power from a US state to its local governments; states vary in how much power they grant.

title: Civil disobedience: Thoreau and King
description: Thoreau argued you should break a law that makes you an agent of injustice; King held there is a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws, openly and accepting the penalty.

facts.text: In 1846 Henry David Thoreau spent a night in jail in Concord, Massachusetts, for refusing to pay his poll tax, in protest against slavery and the Mexican-American War.
Thoreau's essay "Resistance to Civil Government" (1849), later known as "Civil Disobedience", argued that if a law requires you to be "the agent of injustice to another", you should break it.
Thoreau's essay influenced reformers including Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.
In his Letter from Birmingham Jail (16 April 1963), Martin Luther King Jr. wrote that people have a moral responsibility to obey just laws and to disobey unjust ones.
King wrote that one who breaks an unjust law must do so "openly, lovingly, and with a willingness to accept the penalty."
King noted he had been arrested for parading without a permit, and argued that a permit ordinance, fine in itself, becomes unjust when used to maintain segregation.

title: Obeying, and repealing, unjust laws
description: Socrates, in Plato's Crito, chose to obey a sentence he thought unjust because of his implicit agreement with Athens; the legal route out of a law is repeal.

facts.text: In Plato's Crito, Socrates refuses to escape prison before his execution, though he thinks his sentence unjust, arguing that by living in Athens all his life he had implicitly agreed to obey its laws.
South Africa's Population Registration Act of 1950 classified all South Africans by race; it was repealed by a new act of parliament in 1991.

title: Civil law and common law
description: Civil law, from Roman law, starts from written codes such as the Napoleonic Code; common law, from medieval England, builds on judges' precedents.

facts.text: Civil law, the tradition of continental Europe, traces back to Roman law as compiled under Emperor Justinian; France's Napoleonic Code of 1804 became a model for many nations.
Civil law systems are used in continental Europe, much of Latin America, parts of Asia and Africa, and in Quebec and Louisiana.
Civil law systems are based on comprehensive written codes, while common law relies on judge-made precedent: judges follow earlier decisions so similar cases are decided alike.
Common law grew up in medieval England from judges' decisions recorded in reports of decided cases, and is the basis of law in the United States and most Commonwealth countries.

title: Legal traditions around the world
description: Beyond civil and common law are customary and Muslim law, and many countries mix traditions, like bijural Canada.

facts.text: Canada is bijural: in Quebec, private law follows the civil law tradition, set out mainly in the Civil Code of Quebec, while the rest of Canada uses common law.
The University of Ottawa's JuriGlobe project sorts the world's legal systems into five categories: civil law, common law, customary law, Muslim law and mixed systems.
Most Muslim-majority countries adopted Western-style criminal codes but keep sharia mainly for family law, such as marriage, divorce and inheritance; Turkey replaced it with secular codes.
JuriGlobe lists South Africa, Scotland, Louisiana and Quebec as mixes of civil and common law, and Ghana and Kenya as mixes of common and customary law.

title: The word legislator
description: A legislator is literally a "proposer of a law", from Latin legis lator.

facts.text: The word legislator comes from Latin legis lator, "proposer of a law", from lex (law) and lator (proposer), from a verb meaning to carry.

title: What courts do
description: Courts settle disputes peacefully: they find the facts, apply the law to them, and appeal courts check that the law was applied correctly.

facts.text: A court is a person or body with the authority to hear and resolve disputes; its first job is keeping the peace as an impartial, authoritative judge.
Without courts to settle disputes, Britannica notes, people would settle them by force.
Trial courts resolve disputes by working out the facts and applying the law to those facts.
Appeal courts check whether the law was applied correctly in the trial court.

title: Valencia's Water Tribunal
description: A court of elected farmers that has settled irrigation disputes at Valencia Cathedral's door since al-Andalus: oral, impartial and final.

facts.text: Valencia's Water Tribunal meets every Thursday at noon at the door of Valencia Cathedral to settle irrigation disputes.
Valencia's Water Tribunal is a traditional water court dating back to al-Andalus (9th to 13th centuries); UNESCO listed it as intangible heritage in 2009.
The Water Tribunal's eight judges are farmers elected by their irrigation communities, and they wear traditional farmers' blouses.
The Water Tribunal's proceedings are entirely oral, in Valencian, and verdicts are given on the spot.
To keep the Water Tribunal impartial, the syndic of the canal the disputing farmers belong to takes no part in the deliberation.
There is no appeal from the Water Tribunal: its sentence is final.

title: What judges do
description: In a trial the judge keeps it fair, rules on the law, directs the jury and passes sentence.

facts.text: In an English Crown Court trial, the judge makes sure the trial is fair, resolves legal issues, directs the jury on the law and imposes sentence.

title: Judicial independence
description: Judges must be free from pressure: England's Act of Settlement (1701) ended dismissal at the king's pleasure, and the UN's 1985 Basic Principles set a worldwide standard.

facts.text: In 1686, after James II had replaced a number of judges, the court in Godden v Hales upheld his power to excuse individuals from the Test Oath required for public office.
England's Act of Settlement (1701) gave senior judges office during good behaviour, not at the monarch's pleasure; only both Houses of Parliament could remove them.
The Act of Settlement also required judges' salaries to be fixed, so they could not be squeezed with money.
The UN's 1985 Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary say judges must decide impartially, on facts and law, free of improper pressures or threats.

title: How juries work
description: Ordinary citizens chosen at random decide guilt while the judge handles the law; countries such as Japan mix citizens and judges on one panel.

facts.text: In an English Crown Court trial, a jury of 12 members of the public decides whether the defendant is guilty.
Jurors in England and Wales are chosen at random from the electoral register.
Trial by jury grew up in medieval England and spread with the British Empire; the jury decides the facts, the judge the law.
Since 2009, Japan's saiban-in system has six citizens sit with three professional judges in serious criminal cases, deciding guilt and sentence together.

title: Bushel's Case and jury independence
description: In 1670 jurors who acquitted William Penn were punished; Bushel's Case ruled that jurors cannot be punished for their verdict.

facts.text: In 1670 a London jury acquitted the Quakers William Penn and William Mead, charged over preaching; the jurors were held without food, then fined and jailed.
In Bushel's Case (1670), Chief Justice John Vaughan ruled that jurors cannot be punished for their verdict: the court judges the law, the jury the facts.

title: The presumption of innocence
description: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt: Woolmington's 'golden thread', Blackstone's ratio and Article 11 of the UDHR.

facts.text: Reginald Woolmington said the gun that killed his wife went off by accident; his trial judge told the jury it was for him to prove the accident.
In 1935 the House of Lords quashed Woolmington's murder conviction because the burden of proof had been put on the accused.
Viscount Sankey called the prosecution's duty to prove the prisoner's guilt the 'golden thread' running through the web of English criminal law.
In criminal cases the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; if a reasonable doubt remains, the accused is acquitted.
William Blackstone wrote in his Commentaries (1760s) that it is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer.
Article 11 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) gives everyone charged with a penal offence the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty.

title: Prosecution and defence
description: A prosecutor brings the case for the state; a defence lawyer represents the accused, and England's cab-rank rule means barristers can't pick clients by their opinions.

facts.text: In England and Wales, the Crown Prosecution Service, independent of the police, decides which police-investigated cases go to court and prosecutes them.
Under England's cab-rank rule, barristers must generally accept suitable cases whatever they think of the client or cause, so everyone can get legal advice.

title: Gideon and the right to a lawyer
description: Clarence Earl Gideon's handwritten petition led the U.S. Supreme Court in 1963 to require lawyers for poor felony defendants.

facts.text: Clarence Earl Gideon, charged in 1961 with breaking into a Florida pool hall, asked for a lawyer; Florida only appointed lawyers in capital cases, so he defended himself.
Convicted and sent to prison, Gideon sent the U.S. Supreme Court a handwritten petition.
In 1963 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unanimously that states must provide a lawyer to defendants in felony cases who cannot afford one.
At his retrial, Gideon's lawyer discredited the prosecution's key witness, and the jury acquitted him.

title: Criminal versus civil cases
description: Criminal cases are brought by the state and can end in punishment; civil cases settle disputes between parties, with a lower standard of proof.

facts.text: Criminal cases come to court when the state decides to prosecute an alleged crime; sentences include prison, community punishment or a fine.
Civil cases are disputes between people, businesses or organisations, such as damaged goods or debts; the winner may get damages (money) or a court order.
Civil cases use a lower standard of proof: the claim must be more likely than not to be true, over 50% (the balance of probabilities).
In 1995 a jury acquitted O.J. Simpson of murdering Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.
In a 1997 civil trial, Simpson was found liable for the two deaths and ordered to pay $33.5 million in damages to the families.

title: Judicial review
description: Courts can strike down laws that break the constitution: all U.S. courts since Marbury v Madison, special constitutional courts in countries like Germany; UK courts can only declare incompatibility.

facts.text: Judicial review is the power of courts to examine government actions and laws and declare those that break the constitution null and void.
In Marbury v Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall established judicial review in the United States.
In the U.S. any court can hear a constitutional challenge; many European countries, such as Germany and Austria, give that job to a special constitutional court.
UK courts must apply Acts of Parliament even if they breach human rights; higher courts can only declare a law incompatible.
A declaration of incompatibility does not change the law or its enforcement; it is up to Parliament whether to fix it.

title: Germany's constitutional complaint
description: Anyone in Germany can ask the Federal Constitutional Court to protect their fundamental rights; thousands do each year and few succeed.

facts.text: In 2024 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court received 4,640 new cases; about 96% were constitutional complaints.
Any person can lodge a constitutional complaint in Germany claiming a public authority violated their fundamental rights; the court can declare a law void.
About two-thirds of Germany's 2024 constitutional complaints were lodged without a lawyer, and fewer than 2 in 100 complaints succeed.

title: What police do: policing by consent
description: Modern policing began in London in 1829 with unarmed officers; British policing rests on public consent and the prevention of crime.

facts.text: The Metropolitan Police Act 1829, sponsored by Home Secretary Robert Peel, set up a professional police force for London.
London's first police carried only truncheons, handcuffs and a rattle, and wore a blue tailcoat and top hat to show they were not soldiers.
British 'policing by consent' means police power comes from the common consent of the public: 'the police are the public and the public are the police'.
The first of the British policing principles is to prevent crime and disorder, as an alternative to repression by military force.

title: Limits on police power
description: Police powers are limited by law: time limits on detention, rights in custody, the Miranda warnings, and in England and Wales few officers are armed.

facts.text: In England and Wales, police can generally hold someone for up to 24 hours before they must charge or release them; longer needs approval for a serious crime.
People in police custody in England and Wales have the right to free legal advice and to tell someone where they are.
In Miranda v Arizona (1966), the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that police must tell suspects in custody of their right to remain silent and to a lawyer before questioning.
