On 31 March 2026, England and Wales had 6,558 armed police officers: 4.0% (about 4 in 100) of all police officers, Home Office figures show.

title: The purposes of punishment
description: Punishment is justified by retribution, deterrence, incapacitation or rehabilitation; Norway's normality principle leans toward rehabilitation.

facts.text: The main aims given for punishment are retribution (paying for the wrong), deterrence, incapacitation (keeping offenders from reoffending) and rehabilitation (reform); they often conflict.
Norway's prisons follow a 'principle of normality': the punishment is the loss of liberty, and life inside should resemble life outside as much as possible.

title: The punishment debate
description: Retributivists like Kant say punishment is deserved; Bentham said it is justified only if it prevents greater harm; Beccaria stressed certainty over severity.

facts.text: Retributivists such as Immanuel Kant argue punishment is justified because the wrongdoer deserves it, not because of its effects.
Jeremy Bentham wrote that all punishment is in itself evil, justified only as far as it prevents some greater evil.
In On Crimes and Punishments (1764), Cesare Beccaria argued that the certainty of punishment deters more than its severity.

title: Prisons in numbers
description: About 11.7 million people were in prison worldwide in 2023, around 30 per cent of them not yet sentenced.

facts.text: About 11.7 million people were in prison worldwide in 2023, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime.
Around 30 per cent of the world's prisoners, more than 3.7 million people, are in pre-trial detention: held without having been sentenced.

title: Lady Justice's symbols
description: Justice's scales stand for impartial weighing, her sword for power, and her blindfold (from the 16th century) for impartiality; the Old Bailey's statue has none.

facts.text: The gilded statue of Justice on London's Old Bailey holds a sword and scales and, unlike most statues of Justice, wears no blindfold.
Justice comes from a Roman virtue; her scales came to stand for impartiality and her sword for power.
Justice was often shown blindfolded from the 16th century, and the blindfold is now read as a symbol of impartiality.

title: What elections are for: choosing and removing
description: Schumpeter (1942) saw democracy as a competitive struggle for the people's vote, in which voters choose who rules; Popper (1945) saw its test in the ruled dismissing rulers without bloodshed.

facts.text: Joseph Schumpeter, in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), defined the democratic method as one in which people acquire the power to decide through a 'competitive struggle for the people's vote'.
On Schumpeter's view, citizens do not really rule: elections are a fairly peaceful way of keeping or changing those who rule.
Karl Popper, in The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), held that in a democracy the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, for example through general elections.
Popper wrote that 'the people do not rule anywhere, it is always governments that rule'; what matters is a regular, nonviolent way to get rid of bad leaders.

title: The will of the people as the basis of authority
description: Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) makes the will of the people the basis of government authority, expressed in periodic and genuine elections held by secret vote.

facts.text: Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, proclaimed in 1948, says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) says elections shall be held by secret vote or by equivalent free voting procedures.

title: The secret ballot
description: Open voting invited intimidation and bribery. Victoria introduced the modern secret ballot in 1856, South Australia added the X, and Britain adopted it in 1872, so no one can punish a voter for their choice.

facts.text: At Australia's first parliamentary elections, for the New South Wales Legislative Council in 1843, voting was open: voters told an officer out loud who they voted for, often at pubs, amid intimidation and bribery such as free drinks.
Victoria's secret ballot law took effect on 19 March 1856, the first modern secret ballot: voters marked a government-printed ballot paper in private, folded it and put it in a box.
South Australia soon changed the method so voters marked an X beside their chosen candidate instead of crossing out the others; this version is called the Australian ballot.
A secret ballot keeps each voter's choice private so that no one can intimidate them or punish them for how they voted.
Britain's Ballot Act of 1872 introduced the secret ballot, ending open voting that had become associated with bribery, intimidation and drunken disorder.

title: Mill's case against the secret ballot
description: John Stuart Mill (1861) argued a vote is power over others and so a public trust, to be exercised under the eye and criticism of the public; secrecy, he feared, invites selfish voting.

facts.text: In Considerations on Representative Government (1861), John Stuart Mill argued that voting, like any public duty, should be performed 'under the eye and criticism of the public'.
Mill held that a vote is power over others and so a trust for the public; he feared a secret ballot would lead voters to treat it as their own, for their personal benefit.

title: First-past-the-post
description: Under first-past-the-post each district elects the candidate with the most votes. It is simple and gives a local member and often single-party government, but can exclude smaller parties and tends toward two parties (Duverger).

facts.text: In New Zealand's 1978 and 1981 elections, Labour won more votes nationwide than National, but National won more seats and stayed in government, which intensified criticism of the voting system.
Under first-past-the-post, each district elects one member: the candidate with more votes than any other, even without a majority.
First-past-the-post is used mainly in the UK and countries historically influenced by Britain, including Canada, India and the United States.

Reynolds, Reilly and Ellis's IDEA handbook lists FPTP's strengths as simplicity, a local representative and single-party governments, and among its flaws that it shuts smaller parties out of fair representation.
French political scientist Maurice Duverger observed in the 1950s that plurality voting in single-member districts tends to favour a two-party system.

title: Proportional representation
description: Proportional representation turns each party's share of votes into a matching share of seats, using multi-member districts. It wastes few votes and admits smaller parties but often brings coalitions. New Zealand adopted MMP after a 1986 Royal Commission.

facts.text: Proportional representation deliberately turns a party's share of the votes into a matching share of seats, using districts that elect several members; in Israel and the Netherlands the whole country is one district.
The IDEA handbook says PR wastes very few votes and lets smaller parties win seats, but critics say it tends to produce coalition governments and fragmented party systems.

A Royal Commission recommended in 1986 that New Zealand adopt Germany's mixed member proportional system (MMP), giving each voter one vote for a local MP and one for a party; New Zealand first voted under MMP in 1996.

title: Ranked voting
description: Ranked systems let voters number candidates. The Alternative Vote (Australia's House of Representatives) transfers votes until someone has a majority; the Single Transferable Vote (Ireland) does so in multi-member districts. Arrow (1951) proved no ranking method meets every fairness condition.

facts.text: Under the Alternative Vote, used for Australia's House of Representatives, voters rank candidates; if no one has a majority, the least successful are eliminated and their votes transferred by next preference until someone does.
Ireland uses the Single Transferable Vote, in which voters rank candidates in districts that elect several members, keeping results fairly proportional.
Economist Kenneth Arrow proved in 1951 that no method of combining voters' rankings can meet a short list of reasonable fairness conditions all at once; he won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1972.

title: Drawing district boundaries
description: Where members are elected by district, where the lines fall can change results. Boundaries are redrawn as populations change; Canada has used independent commissions chaired by judges since 1964.

facts.text: In an MIT Election Lab illustration, the same 100 voters, split 50-50 between two parties across four districts, can give a 2-2 seat split or a 3-1 win for either party, depending only on where the lines are drawn.
Canada readjusts its federal electoral boundaries after every 10-year census to reflect changes in population.

Since the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act of 1964, independent commissions, one per province and each chaired by a judge, draw Canada's federal districts; sitting legislators cannot serve on them.

title: Gerrymandering
description: Gerrymandering is deliberately drawing district lines to help or hurt a political interest, named after Elbridge Gerry's 1812 salamander district. Packing and cracking waste a group's votes; the efficiency gap measures wasted votes, while Chen and Rodden show geography alone can create bias.

facts.text: The word gerrymander comes from 1812, when Massachusetts governor Elbridge Gerry signed a bill creating oddly shaped districts that helped his party; a Boston Gazette cartoon drew one as a salamander, the 'Gerry-mander'.
Gerrymandering is the deliberate drawing of electoral district boundaries to help or hurt a particular political interest.
Packing crowds a group's voters into as few districts as possible; cracking spreads them thinly across many districts. Both leave that group with fewer seats.

Law professor Nicholas Stephanopoulos and researcher Eric McGhee (2015) proposed the efficiency gap, which compares each party's 'wasted' votes: votes for losers and votes beyond what a winner needed.

Political scientists Jowei Chen and Jonathan Rodden (2013) found that when one party's voters are concentrated in cities, maps drawn without partisan intent can still give it fewer seats than its share of votes.

title: What campaigns do: Lazarsfeld's findings
description: Lazarsfeld's 1940 Erie County study (The People's Choice, 1944) found radio and print had only minor direct effects on votes; people decided mainly through conversations, and ideas flowed through opinion leaders in a two-step flow.

facts.text: In 1940, Paul Lazarsfeld and colleagues interviewed the same voters again and again in Erie County, Ohio, through a US presidential campaign; the study became the 1944 book The People's Choice.
Contrary to their expectations, the researchers found radio and newspapers had only minor direct effects on how people voted; people mainly decided through conversations with those around them.
Lazarsfeld's two-step flow: ideas move from the media to opinion leaders, and then from them to their followers through personal networks.

title: Campaign spending rules
description: Countries set different rules for campaign money: the UK caps party spending in the year before a general election, while the US Supreme Court in Buckley v. Valeo (1976) allowed contribution limits but struck down spending limits.

facts.text: UK law limits how much each party may spend in the 365 days before a general election, with the limit rising with the number of seats it contests.
In Buckley v. Valeo (1976), the US Supreme Court upheld limits on contributions to campaigns but struck down limits on campaign spending as restrictions on free expression.

title: Poll samples: who you ask matters
description: In 1936 the Literary Digest's 2.4 million replies wrongly predicted Landon because its sample leaned to the well-off and few replied; Gallup's scientific sampling called Roosevelt's win.

facts.text: In 1936 the Literary Digest mailed about 10 million straw ballots, got 2.4 million back and predicted Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt; Roosevelt won easily.
The Digest drew its sample from phone lists, car registrations and club memberships, which during the Depression leaned toward the well-off, and only about a quarter of those mailed replied.
George Gallup, using more systematic, scientific sampling, publicly predicted in 1936 that Roosevelt would win re-election handily.

title: Margin of error
description: A margin of plus or minus 3 points at 95% confidence (about 1,067 random interviews) means the result would land within 3 points of the truth 95 times in 100. The margin on a lead is about double, and sampling is only one source of error.

facts.text: A margin of error of plus or minus 3 points at 95% confidence means that if the same survey were run 100 times, the result would be within 3 points of the true value about 95 times.
A simple random sample of 1,067 people has a margin of error of about plus or minus 3 percentage points for a candidate's overall support.
The margin of error on the gap between two candidates is roughly double: a 3-point margin for each becomes about 6 points for a lead, so a 5-point lead could really be anywhere from -1 to +11.
Sampling error is only one of many possible sources of error in polls; question wording and who is less likely to be reached or respond also affect results.

title: Referendums and initiatives
description: A referendum puts a specific question referred by governing institutions directly to voters; a citizens' initiative is started by the people through a petition. Results may be binding or advisory. New Zealand chose MMP by binding referendum in 1993.

facts.text: A referendum gives people a direct vote, binding or advisory, on a specific issue referred to them by governing institutions such as a parliament or president.
A citizens' initiative is a direct vote started by the people themselves, typically through a petition signed by a set number of people.
In practice, advisory referendums are usually treated as politically binding, especially when the result is decisive.
In a binding referendum in 1993, 53.9% of New Zealand voters chose MMP over first-past-the-post.

title: The referendum debate
description: Elliot Bulmer's IDEA primer weighs referendums: they let people vote on a single measure, but voters may respond to unrelated factors, tire of frequent votes, and rulers may use them for false legitimacy, though Pinochet lost one in 1988. The Venice Commission requires clear, non-leading questions.

facts.text: In 1988, Chile's authoritarian ruler Augusto Pinochet unexpectedly lost a referendum to extend his term, and his regime collapsed shortly after.
Elliot Bulmer's International IDEA primer says referendums let citizens vote on a single measure on its own merits, instead of only choosing a party's whole package of policies.

Bulmer also lists criticisms: voters may be swayed by unrelated factors such as how popular party leaders are, frequent votes can cause voter fatigue, and rulers can use referendums to fake legitimacy.
The Council of Europe's Venice Commission says a referendum question must be clear, must not be misleading and must not suggest an answer.

title: Counting in the open
description: Votes are counted where candidates' agents can watch. In the UK, agents observe the verification and count, may request a recount, and a genuine tie is settled by drawing lots.

facts.text: At UK elections, candidates can appoint counting agents to watch the verification and count, and the count is meant to be transparent.
A candidate's agent may ask for a recount; the returning officer must consider it but may refuse an unreasonable request, and any recount happens in full view of those present.
If candidates tie and one more vote would decide the result, the returning officer must decide between them by drawing lots.

title: Checking the count
description: Paper records let counts be checked: India's VVPAT shows each voter a paper slip for 7 seconds. Philip Stark's risk-limiting audits hand-check random ballots and escalate to a full hand count if needed.

facts.text: In India, a VVPAT printer attached to each voting machine shows the voter a paper slip with the candidate's name and symbol for 7 seconds; it then drops into a sealed box, where the slips can be counted.

Statistician Philip Stark developed risk-limiting audits in 2007: officials hand-check randomly chosen paper ballots, and if the sample doesn't confirm the result, the audit grows up to a full hand count, which replaces the reported result.
Risk-limiting audits have been tested in California, Ohio and Denmark.
Stark compares ballot-polling audits to exit polls, noting that 'unlike voters, ballots have to reply, and have to reply truthfully.'

title: Misinformation, disinformation, malinformation
description: Wardle and Derakhshan (Council of Europe, 2017) separate false information shared without intent to harm (misinformation), false information shared to harm (disinformation) and genuine information shared to harm (malinformation).

facts.text: In a 2017 Council of Europe report, Claire Wardle and Hossein Derakhshan separated misinformation (false, shared without meaning harm), disinformation (false, shared knowingly to cause harm) and malinformation (genuine, shared to cause harm).

title: Lateral reading
description: Wineburg and McGrew found fact checkers read laterally, leaving a site to see what others say about it, while historians and students read vertically and were fooled by logos and domain names.

facts.text: Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew watched 10 PhD historians, 10 professional fact checkers and 25 Stanford undergraduates judge live websites on social and political issues.
Historians and students often fell for official-looking logos and domain names, and read vertically, staying on a website to judge whether it was reliable.
Fact checkers read laterally: after a quick scan they left the site and opened new tabs to see what others said about it, reaching better-founded conclusions in a fraction of the time.

title: The SIFT method
description: Mike Caulfield's SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims, quotes and media to the original context, since much online content has been stripped of context.

facts.text: Mike Caulfield's SIFT method has four moves: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims, quotes and media back to the original context.
Caulfield's first move: when you first hit a page or post, stop and ask whether you know what the source is before reading or sharing it.
Caulfield notes that much of what we find online has been stripped of context, like a video clip that leaves out what happened before.

title: Criteria for free and fair elections
description: The IPU's Declaration on Criteria for Free and Fair Elections (Paris, 26 March 1994) grounds authority in the will of the people and lists a secret vote, equal weight, equal campaigning and an honest, observed count.

facts.text: On 26 March 1994 in Paris, the Inter-Parliamentary Council unanimously adopted the Inter-Parliamentary Union's Declaration on Criteria for Free and Fair Elections.
The Declaration says a government's authority can only derive from the will of the people, expressed in genuine, free and fair elections held at regular intervals.

It says the right to vote in secret is absolute, every vote should carry equivalent weight, candidates should campaign on an equal basis, and states should ensure an honest count, with party agents and accredited observers present.

title: Budget: from a leather bag to a spending plan
description: 'Budget' comes from Old French bougette, a little leather bag; in 1733 a pamphlet mocking Walpole's tax plans, The Budget Opened, gave it its money meaning. A government budget sets out the revenue it expects and the spending it plans.

facts.text: 'Budget' comes from Old French bougette, a small leather bag; its financial sense came from the image of a finance minister opening his wallet to reveal his plans.
The financial sense first appeared in 1733 in The Budget Opened, a pamphlet attacking Robert Walpole's tax plans and likening him to a quack; by the 1760s 'budget' was the standard term.
On Budget Day, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer traditionally holds up a red despatch box containing the budget speech.
A government budget is a plan setting out the revenue a government expects to collect and the spending it intends for the coming year.

title: The four-stage budget cycle
description: The budget cycle usually has four stages: the executive prepares the plan, the legislature debates, amends and approves it, the government carries it out, and auditors check the actual spending. The stages of different years overlap.

facts.text: The budget cycle usually has four stages: the executive prepares the plan; the legislature debates, amends and approves it; the government carries it out; and the actual spending is audited and assessed.
Budget cycles overlap: while the executive prepares next year's budget, ministries carry out this year's and the supreme audit institution checks last year's.

title: How big government spending is
description: Across OECD countries, general government spending averaged 42.6% of GDP in 2023; Finland, France and Austria spent over 56% in 2024.

facts.text: General government spending across OECD countries averaged 42.6% of GDP in 2023.
In 2024, public spending was highest in Finland (57.5% of GDP), France (57.2%) and Austria (56.3%).

title: Where the money goes: spending by function
description: Statisticians sort government spending into ten functions (COFOG). Social protection (pensions and sickness, disability and unemployment benefits) is the largest, 13.4% of GDP across the OECD in 2023; health is second.

facts.text: Government spending is classified into ten functions (COFOG), including general public services, defence, public order and safety, economic affairs, health, education and social protection.
Social protection, covering pensions and sickness, disability and unemployment benefits, was the largest area of public spending across OECD countries in 2023, at 13.4% of GDP.
Across the OECD in 2023, health was the second-largest area of public spending at 8.4% of GDP, education averaged 4.9%, and environmental protection was the smallest at 0.5%.
In the EU in 2024, social protection took 40% of all government spending and health 15%; social protection was the largest area in every EU country.
Social protection spending ranged from 7.9% of GDP in the United States to 25.7% in Finland in 2023, which the OECD links to different institutional models.

title: Who runs schools: public and private
description: Public schools are typically funded and regulated by government; private schools are run by a private body. Government-dependent private schools get more than half their money from public sources. The Netherlands funds public and private schools equally.

facts.text: Public schools are typically funded and regulated by government authorities; private schools are under the control of a private body, whatever their funding.
Government-dependent private schools receive more than half their funding from public sources; independent private schools rely mainly on private funding such as fees and donations.
In the Netherlands, the state funds public-authority schools and private schools equally; private schools are usually run by foundations based on religious or other beliefs.
In the Netherlands, private schools are exclusively or largely government-dependent.

title: Paying for schools: how much and which level
description: OECD governments spent 2.2% of GDP on primary and lower secondary schools in 2022. Some countries fund schools from the centre (Greece, Iceland, New Zealand); in Spain and Switzerland, regions or cantons do most of it.

facts.text: In 2022, OECD governments spent on average 2.2% of GDP on primary and lower secondary schools; Iceland spent the most, 3.2%.
Luxembourg spends among the most per primary and lower secondary pupil but falls below the OECD average as a share of GDP, because its GDP per person is among the highest.

Public funding for upper secondary schools is fully centralised in Greece, Iceland and New Zealand, while in Spain over 80% comes from and is managed by regional governments and in Switzerland 94% is spent by the cantons.

title: Ways countries pay for healthcare
description: Countries finance healthcare mainly through government schemes funded by taxes (Nordic countries, UK), compulsory health insurance funded by contributions (France, Germany, Japan), and out-of-pocket payments; most mix them. The WHO's goal is universal health coverage.

facts.text: Government health schemes entitle people to care based on residency and are funded mostly from general taxes; they cover 80% or more of health spending in Sweden, Norway, Iceland, Denmark and the United Kingdom.
In France, Germany, Luxembourg and Japan, more than three-quarters of health spending goes through compulsory health insurance, financed mainly by contributions from employers and employees.
In 2023, households paid more than a third of all health costs directly, out of pocket, in Mexico, Chile, Latvia and Greece.
The WHO defines universal health coverage as all people having access to the quality health services they need, when and where they need them, without financial hardship.

title: How much countries spend on health
description: OECD countries spent on average 9.3% of GDP on health in 2024; the United States spent 17.2% and Germany 12.3%. Health took 15.1% of government spending in 2023.

facts.text: In 2024, OECD countries spent on average 9.3% of GDP on health; the United States spent the most, 17.2%, followed by Germany at 12.3%.
Health accounted for 15.1% of total government spending across OECD countries in 2023.

title: Public pensions: a big bill
description: Germany's 1889 state pension began at 70. Public pensions now average 8.1% of GDP across the OECD and 18% of government spending, from about 16% of GDP in Greece and Italy to under 3% in Iceland and Ireland.

facts.text: Germany's 1889 old-age insurance program, the first national one, set the retirement age at 70; it was lowered to 65 in 1916.
Public spending on old-age and survivors' pensions averaged 8.1% of GDP across the OECD, up from 6.7% in 2000, and made up 18% of total government spending.
Greece and Italy spend around 16% of GDP on public pensions and Iceland and Ireland under 3%; in Iceland and Australia, compulsory workplace schemes provide much retirement income.

title: Ageing and the rising pension age
description: Across the OECD, people aged 65+ per 100 aged 20-64 rose from 22 in 2000 to 33 in 2025 and may reach 52 by 2050. Retirement ages are rising; Denmark confirmed 70 from 2040, a move its government and unions argued over.

facts.text: Across the OECD, the number of people aged 65 and over per 100 people aged 20-64 rose from 22 in 2000 to 33 in 2025 and is projected to reach 52 in 2050.
The OECD uses the old-age to working-age ratio as a proxy for the number of potential pension beneficiaries relative to potential contributors.
Under current laws, the average normal retirement age for men in the OECD will rise from 64.7 years to 66.4 for those starting work in 2024.
In May 2025, Denmark's parliament confirmed raising the state pension age to 70 from 2040, the highest in Europe.
Denmark's government said the rise was needed to afford proper welfare for future generations; unions protested against it as unjust.

title: Infrastructure must be maintained: Genoa's bridge
description: Genoa's Morandi bridge (1967) collapsed on 14 August 2018, killing 43. Its replacement, the San Giorgio bridge (2020), has robots that check it for weathering and erosion.

facts.text: Genoa's Morandi bridge, built in 1967, collapsed on 14 August 2018, killing 43 people.
Its replacement, the San Giorgio bridge designed by Renzo Piano, opened in August 2020 with four robots that run along it checking for weathering and erosion.

title: Paying for roads: user taxes and partnerships
description: Governments pay for roads with taxes, user charges and partnerships. The US Highway Trust Fund (1956) runs on road-user taxes such as fuel tax; PPPs have a private partner fund and deliver a public asset, with mixed audit results.

facts.text: In 1956 the United States set up the Highway Trust Fund as a user-supported fund: highway users pay taxes such as fuel taxes, and the money goes to highway projects, including the Interstate system.
The federal gasoline tax has been 18.4 cents per gallon since 1993.
Since the late 2000s the Highway Trust Fund's taxes have not covered its spending, and Congress has repeatedly transferred extra money into it.
The OECD defines public-private partnerships as long-term agreements in which a private partner delivers and funds public services using a capital asset, sharing the risks.

In 2018 the European Court of Auditors found that PPPs can speed delivery and keep up maintenance, but in its audit of 12 EU-backed PPPs, seven of nine completed projects ran late, by up to 52 months.

title: What corruption is and how it is measured
description: Transparency International defines corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Its 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index scored 182 countries from 0 to 100; the average was 42 and Denmark topped it with 89.

facts.text: Transparency International defines corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain.
Transparency International's 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index scored 182 countries and territories on perceived public-sector corruption, from 0 (highly corrupt) to 100 (very clean).
In the 2025 index the global average fell to 42, 122 countries scored below 50, and Denmark ranked highest for the eighth year in a row, with 89.

title: Fighting corruption: Hong Kong's ICAC
description: In early-1970s Hong Kong, bribes were demanded even for ambulances. After police officer Peter Godber fled in 1973, Hong Kong set up the independent ICAC in 1974, using enforcement, prevention and education.

facts.text: In early-1970s Hong Kong, ambulance crews demanded 'tea money' before picking up a sick person, and bribes were needed for public housing and schooling.
In June 1973, Chief Police Superintendent Peter Godber, under investigation over assets of more than HK$4.3 million, slipped out of Hong Kong, causing a public outcry and a judge-led inquiry.

Hong Kong set up the Independent Commission Against Corruption in February 1974, independent of any government department, with a three-pronged approach of law enforcement, prevention and community education.
In early-1970s Hong Kong, corruption was particularly serious in the police force.
Godber was extradited from England in early 1975, found guilty of conspiracy and accepting bribes, and sentenced to four years in prison.

title: Deficits, surpluses and how debt builds up
description: A government's fiscal balance is revenue minus spending: a deficit when spending is higher. Governments borrow, mostly by selling bonds, to cover deficits, and recurring deficits pile up as debt. In 2023 the average OECD deficit was 4.6% of GDP.

facts.text: A government's fiscal balance is the difference between its revenues and its spending: a surplus when revenue is higher, a deficit when spending is.
Governments borrow to cover deficits, so recurring deficits accumulate as public debt; 79.3% of public debt in OECD countries takes the form of debt securities such as government bonds.
In 2023 the average OECD government ran a deficit of 4.6% of GDP; only six OECD countries had a surplus, led by Norway at 16.5% of GDP.

title: How much debt, and how much is too much
description: The IMF projects global public debt above 100% of GDP by 2029, the highest since 1948. Rich countries with deep bond markets carry high debt at moderate risk; poorer ones can be in distress at lower levels. The IMF and OECD stress different sides.

facts.text: The IMF projects global public debt to rise above 100% of GDP by 2029, its highest level since 1948.

Among the G20, Canada, China, France, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US have public debt above, or projected to exceed, 100% of GDP; the IMF considers their fiscal risk moderate because of their deep, liquid bond markets.
The IMF counts 55 countries in or at high risk of debt distress, often with debt below 60% of GDP, and stresses that the cost of debt matters as well as its size.
The IMF argues that countries should maintain safer debt ratios and build fiscal buffers to use in severe shocks.
The OECD notes that if debt is kept at a sustainable level, deficits can help finance necessary public investment and support living conditions in recessions, pandemics or natural disasters.
Germany's 'debt brake' limits the federal government's structural deficit to 0.35% of GDP; a 2025 reform exempted defence spending above 1% of GDP.

title: Who controls the military
description: In a democracy the armed forces are subordinate to elected civilian authorities, who decide missions, size, budget and purchases; parliaments oversee them through laws, hearings and the purse. Costa Rica's 1949 constitution abolished the army.

facts.text: Article 12 of Costa Rica's 1949 constitution abolishes the army as a permanent institution and provides for the police forces needed to keep public order.
UNESCO notes that Costa Rica invested resources once used for the military in social development, particularly health and education.
Democratic control of armed forces means the military is subordinated to democratically elected authorities and overseen by the courts, the media and civil society.

Under civilian control, civilian authorities decide the military's missions, composition, budget and procurement, while the military keeps operational autonomy in carrying out missions; parliaments oversee through laws, hearings and control of the budget.

title: Military spending around the world
description: SIPRI counts world military spending of $2887 billion in 2025, 2.5% of global GDP; the US, China, Russia, Germany and India made up 58%. NATO members agreed in 2025 to aim for 5% of GDP by 2035.

facts.text: World military spending rose to $2887 billion in 2025, equal to 2.5% of global GDP and on average 6.9% of government spending, according to SIPRI.
The five biggest military spenders in 2025 were the United States, China, Russia, Germany and India, together accounting for 58% of the world total.
In 2014 NATO members agreed to aim for 2% of GDP on defence by 2024; in June 2025 they agreed a target of 5% by 2035, with at least 3.5% for core defence.
SIPRI warns that NATO's broader 5% target could encourage 'creative accounting', with non-military projects reclassified as defence.

title: Auditing public money
description: Supreme audit institutions check how public money was actually spent, the last stage of the budget cycle. The 1977 Lima Declaration, the 'Magna Carta of government auditing', calls for independent government auditing.

facts.text: The Lima Declaration, adopted in 1977 by the world's supreme audit institutions, is known as the Magna Carta of government auditing; its chief aim is to call for independent government auditing.

title: Sovereignty
description: Sovereignty is a state's ultimate authority over its own decisions. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) is often seen as the foundation of the modern system of sovereign states. South Sudan, independent in 2011, is the UN's newest member.

facts.text: South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011, the world's newest country, and the UN General Assembly admitted it as a member state on 14 July 2011.
Britannica defines sovereignty as the ultimate power or authority in the decision-making of the state and in the maintenance of order.

The Peace of Westphalia (1648), negotiated in Munster and Osnabruck, ended the Thirty Years' War in Germany and recognized the full territorial sovereignty of the empire's member states, including the right to make their own treaties.
Many scholars see the Peace of Westphalia as the foundation of the modern system of independent, equal, sovereign states.

title: What counts as a state: the Montevideo criteria
description: The 1933 Montevideo Convention lists four qualifications of a state: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. A state's existence does not depend on recognition.

facts.text: The Montevideo Convention, signed on 26 December 1933, says a state should have a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter into relations with other states.
Article 3 of the Montevideo Convention says the political existence of a state is independent of recognition by other states.

title: Embassies and what diplomats do
description: A diplomatic mission represents its country, protects its interests and citizens, negotiates, reports home and promotes friendly relations. Relations are set up by mutual consent, under rules written down in the 1961 Vienna Convention.

facts.text: Under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, a diplomatic mission represents its country, protects its interests and citizens, negotiates with the host government, reports home on conditions there and promotes friendly relations.
Diplomatic relations between states, and permanent diplomatic missions, are established by mutual consent.
The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, signed on 18 April 1961, wrote down rules of diplomacy that had been stable for over 200 years; almost all states are now parties.
The Vienna Convention's preamble recalls that peoples of all nations from ancient times have recognized the status of diplomatic agents.

title: Diplomatic immunity and its limits
description: Embassy premises are inviolable and diplomats cannot be arrested or tried in the host country's criminal courts, so that missions can do their work. The host can declare a diplomat persona non grata at any time.

facts.text: Under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, an embassy's premises are inviolable: the host country's officials may not enter without the consent of the head of the mission.
A diplomat's person is inviolable: diplomats cannot be arrested or detained and are immune from the host country's criminal courts.

The Vienna Convention says diplomatic immunities exist not to benefit individuals but so that missions can do their work representing states, without coercion or harassment; diplomats must still respect local laws.
A host country may at any time, without explaining why, declare a diplomat persona non grata; the sending country must then recall that person.

title: The Kadesh treaty: the oldest known peace treaty
description: Around 1269 BC the Hittite king Hattusili III and Egypt's Ramesses II made peace in writing: the oldest known peace treaty. A replica hangs at UN Headquarters.

facts.text: The Kadesh peace treaty between the Hittite king Hattusili III and Egypt's Ramesses II, dated by the UN to 1269 BC, is the oldest known peace treaty.
The Kadesh treaty pledges lasting peace, nonaggression, extradition and mutual help; a replica hangs near the entrance of the Security Council Chamber at UN Headquarters.

title: What a treaty is and why it binds
description: A treaty is a written agreement between states governed by international law, whatever it is called. Pacta sunt servanda: a treaty in force binds its parties and must be kept in good faith, and internal law is no excuse.

facts.text: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969) defines a treaty as a written agreement between states governed by international law, whatever its particular name.

Pacta sunt servanda, Latin for 'agreements must be kept', is arguably the oldest principle of international law; Article 26 of the 1969 Vienna Convention says every treaty in force binds its parties and must be performed in good faith.
Under Article 27 of the 1969 Vienna Convention, a party may not use its own internal law as a justification for failing to perform a treaty.

title: Signing and ratifying a treaty
description: For treaties that need ratification, signing does not yet bind a state; ratification is the act by which a state consents to be bound. A signer must not defeat the treaty's purpose in the meantime.

facts.text: When a treaty needs ratification, signing it does not yet bind a state; ratification is the international act by which a state consents to be bound.
After signing a treaty subject to ratification, a state must refrain from acts that would defeat the treaty's object and purpose until it makes clear it will not become a party.

title: The UN's founding, and what it is not
description: The UN Charter opens with a pledge to save future generations from war. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945. It is not a world government: it has no army, levies no taxes and depends on its members.

facts.text: The UN Charter's preamble opens with a determination 'to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war, which twice in our lifetime has brought untold sorrow to mankind'.

Delegates of 50 countries met in San Francisco from 25 April to 26 June 1945 to draw up the UN Charter; the UN came into existence on 24 October 1945, once China, France, the Soviet Union, the UK, the US and most other signatories had ratified it.
The UN says it is neither a supra-state nor a government of governments: it has no army, levies no taxes and depends on the political will and contributions of its member states.

title: The General Assembly: one country, one vote
description: All 193 UN members sit in the General Assembly with one vote each, reflecting the Charter's sovereign equality of members. It makes recommendations; important questions need a two-thirds majority.

facts.text: Article 2 of the UN Charter says the organization is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all its members.
All 193 UN member states sit in the General Assembly, each with one vote; it makes recommendations to states, and important questions need a two-thirds majority.

title: The Security Council and the veto
description: The Security Council has primary responsibility for peace. It has 15 members, 5 of them permanent with a veto: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US. Its decisions bind all UN members.

facts.text: The UN Security Council has primary responsibility for international peace and security; it has 15 members, 5 of them permanent: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

UN members agree to carry out Security Council decisions; a substantive decision needs nine votes including the concurring votes of all five permanent members, so one permanent member's no vote blocks it: the veto.

title: How the EU began: coal, steel and peace
description: In 1950 Robert Schuman proposed pooling coal and steel to make war between France and Germany materially impossible. Six countries signed the coal and steel treaty in 1951, the first step toward today's 27-member EU.

facts.text: On 9 May 1950, French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed pooling Western Europe's coal and steel industries, saying it would make war between France and Germany 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'.

In 1951, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands signed a treaty to run their coal and steel industries jointly, so that no single country could make the weapons of war to turn against the others; it was the first step toward today's European Union.
European cooperation began with the aim of ending the frequent and bloody conflicts between neighbours that culminated in the Second World War.
The European Union has 27 member countries.

title: How the EU makes laws
description: Everything the EU does rests on treaties its members agreed. The Commission proposes laws; the directly elected European Parliament and the Council of national ministers adopt them; member countries implement them.

facts.text: Everything the EU does is founded on treaties voluntarily and democratically agreed by its member countries.
The European Commission proposes new EU laws; the European Parliament, directly elected by EU citizens, and the Council of the EU, where national ministers represent member governments, adopt them.
EU member countries implement the laws, and the European Commission ensures they are properly applied.

title: Why wars start, and the rules on starting them
description: Clausewitz saw war as a continuation of state policy by other means. Rules tightened over time: the 1907 Hague Convention required a declaration, the 1928 Kellogg-Briand Pact renounced war but could not be enforced, and the 1945 UN Charter bans force except self-defence.

facts.text: Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz's On War, published in 1832 after his death, argued that war is a continuation of state policy by other means.
The Hague Convention III of 18 October 1907 required that hostilities not begin without a previous and explicit warning: a reasoned declaration of war or an ultimatum.
In the Kellogg-Briand Pact, signed in Paris on 27 August 1928, countries renounced war as an instrument of national policy, but there was no way to enforce it and it did not prevent World War II.
The UN Charter (1945) requires members to refrain from the threat or use of force against other states, while keeping the inherent right of self-defence if an armed attack occurs.

title: How wars end: armistice and peace treaty
description: An armistice stops the fighting while peace terms are worked out; a peace treaty formally ends a war. The 1918 armistice was followed by the Treaty of Versailles; the 1953 Korean armistice was not a peace treaty.

facts.text: The armistice of 11 November 1918 stopped the fighting on the Western Front but did not end the First World War; the war formally ended with the Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919.
An armistice is an agreement to stop the fighting while the terms of peace are negotiated; a peace treaty formally ends the war.
The Korean War armistice, signed on 27 July 1953, stopped the fighting but was not a permanent peace treaty.

title: The International Court of Justice
description: The ICJ, the UN's principal judicial organ, sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague. Only states can be parties, its jurisdiction rests on their consent, and its 15 judges are elected by the General Assembly and Security Council.

facts.text: The International Court of Justice, the UN's principal judicial organ, sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague; it is the only one of the UN's six main organs not in New York.
The ICJ has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms by the UN General Assembly and Security Council.
Only states may be parties in cases before the ICJ; its jurisdiction rests on the consent of the states involved, and it also gives advisory opinions when UN bodies ask.

title: Trying individuals: Nuremberg and the ICC
description: The Nuremberg tribunal held that crimes against international law are committed by people. The International Criminal Court, in The Hague since 2002, tries individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression, as a court of last resort.

facts.text: The International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, run by the US, UK, Soviet Union and France, tried 22 leading Nazi officials between 20 November 1945 and 1 October 1946, setting precedents for later war crimes trials.
The Nuremberg tribunal's judgment said: 'Crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities.'

The International Criminal Court in The Hague, set up by a treaty called the Rome Statute, tries individuals charged with genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and the crime of aggression, for crimes since 1 July 2002.
The ICC is a court of last resort: it seeks to complement national courts, not replace them.

title: Nansen and the first refugee passport
description: In 1921 the League of Nations made Fridtjof Nansen its first High Commissioner for Refugees. His 1922 Nansen passport let stateless refugees travel to find work; he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

facts.text: In August 1921 the League of Nations appointed Norwegian polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen its first High Commissioner for Refugees, to help people fleeing Russia after the Bolshevik revolution.

In 1922 Nansen won states' agreement to the 'Nansen passport', a travel document for refugees who had lost their nationality that let them travel to other countries to look for work; about 450,000 people used one.
Fridtjof Nansen received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922.

title: Who is a refugee
description: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, a refugee is outside their own country because of a well-founded fear of persecution on one of five grounds. Refugee status is declaratory. Most forcibly displaced people (UNHCR, end-2025) stay inside their own countries.

facts.text: The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee as someone outside their own country who, owing to a well-founded fear of persecution for their race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, cannot or will not accept its protection.
UNHCR says refugee status is declaratory: a person is a refugee from the moment they meet the criteria, whether or not their status has been formally recognized.
UNHCR's Global Trends report counted 117.8 million people forcibly displaced at the end of 2025: 41.6 million refugees and 68.7 million displaced inside their own countries by conflict or violence.

title: Asylum and non-refoulement
description: Asylum is protection a state grants to people fleeing persecution or serious harm; UNHCR calls seeking it a human right. Non-refoulement forbids returning refugees to where their life or freedom would be threatened.

facts.text: Under the principle of non-refoulement (1951 Refugee Convention, Article 33), a refugee must not be expelled or returned to a territory where their life or freedom would be threatened; UNHCR calls it one of the most fundamental principles of international law.
Asylum is protection a state grants to people outside their own country who are seeking safety from persecution or serious harm; UNHCR says seeking asylum is a human right.

title: Problems no country can solve alone
description: The UN calls climate change a global emergency beyond national borders. No nation can cut emissions enough alone, and each can be tempted to free ride on others' efforts: a collective action problem.

facts.text: The UN describes climate change as a global emergency that goes beyond national borders and requires international cooperation.
OpenStax's economics text says no nation by itself can reduce greenhouse gas emissions enough to solve global warming without the cooperation of other nations.

Political scientists describe climate change as a collective action problem: a country can benefit from free riding on other countries' efforts, since the climate changes whether or not it makes sacrifices.

title: The Montreal Protocol
description: The Montreal Protocol (1987) phases out ozone-depleting chemicals. It was the first treaty in UN history ratified by every country; 99 per cent of those chemicals are gone and the ozone layer is recovering.

facts.text: The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987 to phase out the chemicals that deplete the ozone layer, became the first treaty in UN history to be ratified by every country.
Under the Montreal Protocol, 99 per cent of ozone-depleting substances have been phased out.
If current policies hold, the ozone layer is projected to return to 1980 values around 2066 over Antarctica, 2045 over the Arctic and 2040 elsewhere.

title: The Paris Agreement
description: The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to hold warming well below 2 degrees C and pursue 1.5 degrees C. Each country sets its own national plan (an NDC) and updates it every five years.

facts.text: The Paris Agreement, adopted on 12 December 2015, aims to hold global warming well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.
Under the Paris Agreement, each country sets out its own national climate plan, a nationally determined contribution (NDC), and submits an updated one every five years.

title: The Antarctic Treaty: a continent run by agreement
description: Signed in 1959 by twelve countries, the Antarctic Treaty keeps Antarctica for peaceful purposes and science, freezes territorial claims and opens every station to inspection.

facts.text: The Antarctic Treaty was signed in Washington on 1 December 1959 by twelve countries whose scientists had taken part in the International Geophysical Year (1957–58); it entered into force in 1961 and now has 58 parties.

Seven signatories, including Argentina, Chile and the United Kingdom, had claimed parts of Antarctica, some overlapping; Article IV neither denies nor supports the claims and allows no new or enlarged claims while the treaty is in force.

The Antarctic Treaty says Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only, bans military bases and nuclear explosions there, protects freedom of scientific investigation and requires scientific results to be shared.
Under Article VII of the Antarctic Treaty, all areas of Antarctica, including every station, are open to inspection at all times, to check that the treaty is observed.

title: What citizenship is
description: Citizenship is a relationship between a person and a state: the person owes allegiance and is entitled to the state's protection.

facts.text: Britannica defines citizenship as the relationship between an individual and a state to which the individual owes allegiance and in turn is entitled to its protection.

title: Citizenship by birth: soil and blood
description: Jus soli grants citizenship by birthplace; jus sanguinis by a parent's citizenship. Nearly every Western Hemisphere country uses jus soli; Japan uses descent.

facts.text: Jus soli ("right of the soil") grants citizenship to anyone born within a state's territory, regardless of the parents' citizenship.
Jus sanguinis ("right of blood") grants citizenship on the basis of a parent's citizenship, irrespective of where the child is born.
Birthright citizenship (jus soli) is the basis for citizenship in nearly every nation-state in the Western Hemisphere.
Under Japan's nationality law, a child is a Japanese national if the father or mother is a Japanese national at the time of birth.

title: Naturalization
description: Adults can become citizens by applying, usually after residence and a test of language or knowledge; Canada asks for 1,095 days in five years.

facts.text: Naturalization lets a foreign national become a citizen by applying; requirements typically include a period of residence, language skills and knowledge of the country.
Applicants for Canadian citizenship must have been physically in Canada for at least 1,095 days (3 years) during the 5 years before they apply.
Applicants for Canadian citizenship aged 18 to 54 must pass a citizenship test on topics such as rights, history, geography and government.

title: Rights come with responsibilities
description: Citizenship guides pair rights with responsibilities: some are legal duties (obeying the law, jury service when called), others civic ones (voting, helping others).

facts.text: Canada's official citizenship study guide, Discover Canada, says that in Canada, rights come with responsibilities.
Discover Canada lists citizens' responsibilities including obeying the law, serving on a jury, voting in elections, helping others in the community, and protecting heritage and the environment.
Discover Canada says that when you are called to serve on a jury, you are legally required to serve.

title: Compulsory voting in Australia
description: Australia made voting at federal elections compulsory in 1924; turnout rose from under 60% in 1922 to over 91% in 1925.

facts.text: In 1924 Australia amended its electoral law to make voting at federal elections compulsory.
Australians who fail to vote at a federal election without a valid and sufficient reason face a penalty.
Turnout at Australia's 1922 federal election was under 60%; at the 1925 election, the first after voting became compulsory, it rose to over 91%.

title: Contacting your representative
description: A UK MP represents everyone in the constituency, voters or not, handles constituents' issues, and holds surgeries to meet them.

facts.text: UK MPs are elected to represent the interests and concerns of all the people who live in their constituency, whether they voted for them or not.
UK MPs can normally only deal with issues raised by people who live in their constituency, called constituents.
Most UK MPs hold surgeries in their constituency, where people can meet them and discuss matters of concern.

title: Petitions to parliament
description: UK Parliament petitions get a government response at 10,000 signatures and are considered for debate at 100,000; Canadian e-petitions need 500 signatures.

facts.text: UK Parliament petitions that reach 10,000 signatures get a response from the government; those that reach 100,000 are considered for debate in Parliament.
A Canadian House of Commons e-petition needs at least 500 signatures to be presented, and the government responds within 45 days of presentation.

title: What volunteering is
description: Volunteer work is unpaid and non-compulsory, done through organizations (formal) or directly for others (informal); informal volunteering is more than twice as common.

facts.text: The ILO defines volunteer work as unpaid, non-compulsory work: time people give without pay to activities done through an organization or directly for others outside their own household.
Worldwide, more than twice as many people volunteer informally (directly between individuals) as formally (through an organization or association).

title: How much volunteering there is
description: About 862 million people aged 15 and over volunteer each month; the NSW Rural Fire Service shows volunteers delivering a public service.

facts.text: UN Volunteers' 2022 State of the World's Volunteerism Report estimated that 862 million people aged 15 and over volunteer each month.
The NSW Rural Fire Service in Australia, with about 70,000 volunteer members, is widely described as the largest volunteer fire service in the world.

title: Headlines versus stories
description: Many shared links are never read (59% in a 2016 study); press codes forbid headlines not supported by the text, so read past the headline.

facts.text: A 2016 study by researchers at Columbia University and France's Inria found that 59% of the news links shared on Twitter in their sample were never clicked.
The UK Editors' Code, enforced by the press regulator IPSO, says the press must take care not to publish misleading information, including headlines not supported by the text.

title: Signs of reliable reporting
description: Journalism codes ask for clearly identified sources, labeled opinion, and prompt, prominent corrections: clues a reader can check.

facts.text: The Society of Professional Journalists' Code of Ethics says to identify sources clearly, so the public can judge their reliability and motivations.
The SPJ code says to label advocacy and commentary; the UK Editors' Code says the press, while free to campaign, must distinguish clearly between comment, conjecture and fact.
The SPJ code says to acknowledge mistakes and correct them promptly and prominently; the UK Editors' Code says significant inaccuracies must be corrected promptly and with due prominence.

title: Children's right to be heard
description: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) gives children the right to express their views in matters affecting them (Article 12).

facts.text: The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child was adopted by the General Assembly on 20 November 1989 and is the world's most widely ratified human rights treaty.
The Convention defines a child as every human being below the age of 18, unless the law applicable to the child sets adulthood earlier.
Article 12 of the Convention gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting the child, given due weight according to age and maturity.

title: Youth parliaments
description: Youth parliaments let under-18s practice politics: the UK Youth Parliament elects members aged 11 to 18 and debated in the Commons chamber in 2009.

facts.text: Members of the UK Youth Parliament are elected, and any young person aged 11 to 18 can vote or stand; once elected, members run campaigns on issues that matter to young people.
On 30 October 2009, about 300 Members of the UK Youth Parliament debated in the House of Commons chamber, the first time a group other than MPs had used it.

title: How city councils are organized
description: In US cities, the council-manager form has the council hire a professional manager; the mayor-council form has a separately elected mayor with executive power.

facts.text: In the council-manager form of US city government, the elected council makes policy and sets the budget, and appoints a professional city manager to run day-to-day operations.
In the mayor-council form, the mayor is elected separately from the council, is often full-time, and has significant administrative and budgetary authority; the council keeps legislative powers.

title: Local government in public view
description: English council meetings are open to the public, with agendas published five clear days ahead; India's gram sabha includes every village voter.

facts.text: Under the Local Government Act 1972, a meeting of a principal council in England is open to the public, except where the public is lawfully excluded, for example for confidential matters.
The same Act requires a council's agenda and reports to be open to public inspection at least five clear days before the meeting.
In India, the gram sabha is made up of everyone on the electoral roll of a village panchayat, and it approves development plans before the panchayat carries them out.

title: Myth: a higher tax bracket taxes all your income
description: With marginal brackets, as in US and UK income tax, only income inside a higher bracket pays its rate.

facts.text: With marginal income tax brackets, as in the US and the UK, only the part of income within a higher bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate, not the whole income.

title: Myth: every new government brings new officials
description: The UK Civil Service Code requires civil servants to serve any elected government equally well and keep their own politics out of their advice.

facts.text: The UK Civil Service Code requires civil servants to serve the government, whatever its political persuasion, and to serve equally well governments of different political persuasions.
The Civil Service Code says civil servants must not let their personal political views determine any advice they give or their actions.

title: Mill: know the other side
description: In On Liberty (1859), Mill argued you cannot prefer your view without knowing and answering the other side at its strongest.

facts.text: In On Liberty (1859), John Stuart Mill wrote: "He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that."
Mill argued that if you cannot refute the reasons on the opposite side, or do not even know them, you have no ground for preferring either opinion.
Mill said you must hear opposing arguments from people who actually believe them, and know them in their most plausible and persuasive form.

title: Arguing in good faith
description: Rapoport's rules (restate, agree, credit, then criticize) and Graham's hierarchy (from name-calling to refuting the central point) describe how to disagree well.

facts.text: In Intuition Pumps (2013), Daniel Dennett set out rules from game theorist Anatol Rapoport: restate the other view so well its holder says "Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it that way", list points of agreement, mention what you learned, and only then criticize.
Paul Graham's 2008 essay How to Disagree ranks disagreement from name-calling at the bottom, through ad hominem and responding to tone, up to refuting the central point at the top.
